books.title: Frogs and Toads
books.art_why: Real frogs, toads, and natural habitats can be photographed.

pages.text: Have you ever seen an unusual animal in nature? Did you want to learn more about it? Last week I saw a really neat frog, and that was the start of a wonderful adventure. What does a frog say when it sees something great? Toadly awesome!
pages.brief: A curious child stands outdoors in a natural setting, looking closely at a single frog. The child leans in with interest, clearly noticing the unusual animal and wanting to learn more about it. The frog sits calmly nearby.

pages.text: I looked for the frog in a book called a field guide. I started looking through the pictures in the book. I was amazed to see all the different kinds of frogs and toads. It turns out I saw a wood frog. Do You Know? There are almost 5,000 kinds of frogs and toads. The biggest one is as big as a dinner plate. One of the smallest is the Brazilian gold frog. Its real size is shown here.
pages.brief: A child sits at a table, looking through the pictures in an open field guide. The pages show many different kinds of frogs and toads. A wood frog is visible among them. Nearby, a tiny Brazilian gold frog is shown at its real size.

pages.text: I wanted to know more, so I went to the Internet. Did you know that frogs and toads are relatives of newts and salamanders? They’re all amphibians, which means they live part of their life in water and part on land. Amphibians are cold-blooded animals. They don’t make their own body heat. They get warmth from the heat of the sun.
pages.brief: A child sits at a computer, looking at images of frogs, toads, newts, and salamanders. The scene suggests these amphibians live partly in water and partly on land. Sunlight shines on a frog and a salamander, showing how they get warmth from the sun.

pages.text: Life Cycle I also learned that most frogs and toads lay jelly-covered eggs in water. The babies that hatch are called tadpoles and look like little fish. Tadpoles breathe with gills, just like fish, and they live in water. But it’s amazing what happens as they grow!
pages.brief: Jelly-covered eggs float in water. Nearby, newly hatched tadpoles look like little fish, with gills and tails, swimming underwater. The scene focuses on the beginning of the life cycle, with the eggs and tadpoles in their watery habitat.

pages.text: Their gills disappear, and they grow lungs so they can breathe air like other land animals. They grow legs and then arms. Later, their tail shrinks. By the time their tail is gone, they move onto land. I saw some very cool photos of the life cycle of frogs and toads.
pages.brief: A tadpole with tiny legs and a shrinking tail swims near water. Another young amphibian has lungs and legs. A tailless young frog sits on land. The image shows the growing changes from water-breathing tadpole to land-living frog.

pages.text: About Frogs Frogs are famous for their ability to leap with their long, strong back legs. They leap to catch insects and other prey. A frog can catch an insect in an instant with its long, sticky tongue. Why are frogs so good at baseball? Because they catch a lot of flies.
pages.brief: A frog leaps through the air with its long, strong back legs extended. Its long, sticky tongue shoots out to catch an insect. The frog is in a natural outdoor setting, using its leap and tongue to capture prey.

pages.text: The eyes and nostrils of a frog are on the top of its head. Frogs can see, smell, and breathe while they’re mostly under water. In fact, they breathe through their skin while they’re under water! Frogs can make an amazing amount of noise. Male frogs sing loudly to attract a mate. Do You Know? Male frogs use throat pouches to sing. Some male frogs have one throat pouch, and others have two. What has more lives than a cat? A frog—it croaks every night.
pages.brief: A frog sits mostly underwater, with only its eyes and nostrils above the surface. Nearby, a male frog sings loudly with an inflated throat pouch. The water surrounds them, showing how frogs can see, smell, and breathe while mostly submerged.

pages.text: Do you know the differences between frogs and toads? Here’s what I learned from a book at the library. Frogs Toads.
pages.brief: A child sits in a library, looking at an open book. The book shows a frog and a toad side by side, so the child can compare them. The library setting is quiet, with shelves around the child.

pages.text: Defense I was sad to learn that frogs and toads are food for many other animals. Bats, snakes, birds, and rodents all hunt them. But frogs and toads have clever ways to stay safe from animals that might try to eat them. What happens when frogs park illegally? They get toad away.
pages.brief: A frog or toad sits alert in a natural setting. A bat flies overhead, a snake moves nearby, a bird watches, and a rodent is close by. These animals hunt frogs and toads, so the amphibian stays watchful and uses clever defenses.

pages.text: Some frogs and toads, like the wood frog I saw, are the same color as their habitat. This is called blending in. It allows them to hide better from predators. Some kinds of frogs are so poisonous that just touching their skin is deadly. These frogs are brightly colored to warn predators to stay away. Do You Know? One golden poison frog contains enough poison to kill 10 people or 20,000 mice. This frog is one of the most poisonous animals on Earth.
pages.brief: A wood frog blends in with leaves and ground because its color matches its habitat. Nearby, a brightly colored golden poison frog stands out, warning predators to stay away. Both frogs are shown in natural surroundings. The contrast shows hiding and warning.

pages.text: Some frogs try to trick predators that might want to eat them. The tomato frog puffs up like a balloon when a snake gets near. The snake thinks the frog is too big to eat. If the snake tries to eat it anyway, the frog leaks a liquid like glue from its skin.
pages.brief: A tomato frog puffs up like a balloon as a snake comes near. The snake looks at the swollen frog, which appears too big to eat. The frog’s skin looks glossy, suggesting the glue-like liquid it can leak.

pages.text: Why are frogs so happy? They eat whatever bugs them. Frogs Are Cool! Frogs and toads come in many shapes, sizes, and colors. You can find them in trees, in or near water, and on the ground. One thing is true about all of them—they’re amazing animals. What kinds of frogs have you seen?
pages.brief: Several frogs and toads of different shapes, sizes, and colors are shown. One sits in a tree, one is in or near water, and one rests on the ground. The scene shows where these amazing animals can be found.

books.title: You Stink!
books.art_why: Skunks are real animals that can be photographed today.

pages.text: You Stink!
pages.brief: A single skunk fills the page, standing alone in full view and looking straight out. Its soft black fur, long white stripes, short legs and long, bushy tail are clearly visible as it calmly faces the reader.

pages.text: Nobody Likes You! Imagine that you are a four-legged animal about the size of a cat. You have short legs and a long, bushy tail. Your soft black fur has long white stripes. You are a beautiful animal, but nobody wants to be your friend. Why not? You’re a skunk, and you stink! Anyone who smells you or gets sprayed by you never forgets it.
pages.brief: A cat-sized skunk with short legs, a long bushy tail, soft black fur and long white stripes stands by itself. Nearby animals keep their distance, making clear that no one wants to be its friend.

pages.text: You and your smelly cousins live in many parts of North and South America. Striped skunks—your kind—are the skunks most people know about. Hooded skunks look like you, but more of their fur is white. Hog-nosed skunks look like hooded skunks with long noses. Spotted skunks have white spots or short stripes. Do You Know? Not all skunks are black and white. Some skunks are white with brown, tan, or gray. A few skunks are all white.
pages.brief: A map of North and South America shows where skunks live. Several skunks are shown: a striped skunk, a hooded skunk with more white fur, a hog-nosed skunk with a long nose, and a spotted skunk with white spots or short stripes. A few skunks appear all white.

pages.text: What Kind of Animal? You are a mammal. This large group also includes whales, bears, deer, mice, and many other animals. Like other mammals, you have a backbone and hair, and your babies are born live. The mammals on this page are some of your closest relatives.
pages.brief: A skunk is shown with other mammals—a whale, a bear, a deer and a mouse—to show the large mammal group. The animals have backbones and hair, and a mother mammal is shown with a baby born live.

pages.text: Like many of your relatives, you like to eat both animals and plants. More than half of your food is insects. You also like to eat worms, frogs, rodents, lizards, snakes, birds, and eggs. Some of your favorite plants are grass, leaves, nuts, and berries. Do You Know? Skunks eat garbage in areas where people live. They also eat dead animals left behind by cats. Skunks eat different foods at different times of the year. They don’t care what they eat as long as it fills them up.
pages.brief: A skunk searches for food, eating insects, worms, a frog, a rodent, a lizard, a snake, a bird and eggs. Nearby are grass, leaves, nuts and berries. In an area where people live, it also noses through garbage.

pages.text: Why You Stink You have a secret weapon to keep enemies away. You only use it after you try everything else. First, you stamp your feet if an enemy comes close. Then you hiss and growl. If the enemy doesn’t leave, you raise your tail and arch your back. You try to look bigger to scare the enemy.
pages.brief: An enemy comes close to a skunk. The skunk first stamps its feet, then hisses and growls. If the enemy stays, the skunk raises its tail, arches its back and tries to look bigger to scare it away.

pages.text: Sometimes these warnings do not work. Then you spray your enemy with a sticky, smelly liquid called musk. Musk comes from a pouch at the bottom of your tail. Musk smells worse than terrible. It takes a long time for the strong smell to go away. Do You Know? Skunks spray dogs that get too close to them. People wash their dogs with tomato juice to help get rid of the smell.
pages.brief: A skunk sprays a sticky, smelly liquid called musk from a pouch at the bottom of its tail toward a dog that has come too close. Later, a person washes the dog with tomato juice to remove the strong smell.

pages.text: What animals are enemies of you and your stinky cousins? Most other mammals leave you alone. Your black-and-white fur is a warning to keep away. But some large animals think of you as a tasty meal. Great horned owls are your worst enemy. They have a very poor sense of smell.
pages.brief: A great horned owl swoops near a skunk. The skunk’s black-and-white fur acts as a warning, and most other mammals stay away, but the owl has a very poor sense of smell and sees the skunk as a tasty meal.

pages.text: Skunk Homes Your home is called a den. You might make your home inside a hollow log. Many of your cousins live in underground burrows. If you live near people, you may live under a house. You are careful not to spray musk around your home. You don’t like your smell any more than other animals do!
pages.brief: A skunk sits at the entrance to its den inside a hollow log. Other skunks are in underground burrows, and one den is under a house near people. The skunk is careful not to spray musk around its home.

pages.text: You spend winter in your den, but you don’t sleep all winter as bears do. On warmer days, you come out to look for food. You don’t spend much time with other skunks. But on cold winter days, many of you gather together in a den to keep warm. Do You Know? Skunks sleep during the day. They look for food when the Sun starts to go down. Their worst enemy, the great horned owl, is active at night, too.
pages.brief: In winter, skunks gather together in a den to keep warm on cold days. On warmer days, one skunk comes out to look for food. Skunks sleep during the day and become active when the Sun goes down, when the great horned owl is also active.

pages.text: Baby Skunks If you are a female skunk, you give birth to babies in the spring. The babies are called kits. You usually have five or six kits at one time. Your kits are born with skin that is black and white. Their skin has the same pattern of color that their fur will have someday.
pages.brief: A female skunk rests in her den in spring with five or six newborn kits close to her body. The babies’ skin is black and white, with the same color pattern their fur will have someday.

pages.text: You stay in your den with your kits for about six weeks. Like other mammals, you feed your babies milk so they will grow. Then you take your kits outside. You protect them from animals that might want to eat them. Your kits learn how to find food and stay safe. After nearly a year, they leave you to live alone.
pages.brief: A mother skunk stays in the den with her kits for about six weeks and feeds them milk. Later she takes them outside, protects them from animals that might eat them, and teaches them to find food and stay safe. After nearly a year, the kits leave.

pages.text: Skunks and People You and your smelly cousins want people to leave you alone. If people come too close, you might spray them. You might try to bite or scratch, too. Some of your cousins have a sickness called rabies. Rabies can kill people. This is another good reason for people to leave you alone. But the biggest reason is because you stink! Do You Know? Some people keep skunks as pets. Usually, these pets are not stinky. A doctor removes the part that makes musk.
pages.brief: A skunk faces people who keep their distance. If people come too close, the skunk might spray, bite or scratch. Some skunks carry rabies, which can kill people. A pet skunk is shown with a doctor who has removed the part that makes musk.

books.title: How Much Is a Trillion?
books.art_why: The book uses real-world examples such as cities, people, pennies, buses, and a football field that can be photographed.

pages.text: How Much Is a Trillion?
pages.brief: A bright cover-style illustration introduces the idea of enormous numbers, with simple bold shapes and scattered zero-like forms filling a wide sky above an open horizon, creating a playful sense of scale for young readers.

pages.text: How Much How Much Is a Trillion? Is a Trillion?
pages.brief: A second cover-style illustration repeats the sense of huge scale, showing broad bands of color and simple rounded shapes that suggest counting higher and higher across an open, uncluttered background for young readers with an inviting feel.

pages.text: Really Big Numbers What’s the biggest number you can think of? One hundred? One thousand? Ten thousand? We use special words such as million, billion, and trillion to talk about really big numbers. But what do these words mean? And what do a million, a billion, and a trillion look like?
pages.brief: Large clusters of simple zero shapes fill a bright scene, arranged to suggest million, billion, and trillion, with open space around them as if inviting a young reader to imagine the biggest number they can think of.

pages.text: Hide and Seek Have you ever played the game of hide and seek? In hide and seek, one person counts up to a number while everyone else hides. But some numbers are so big that you couldn’t count up to them in your whole lifetime.
pages.brief: Children play hide and seek outdoors in a sunny park, with one child counting at a tree while others run to hide behind bushes and fences, showing how counting to enormous numbers would take a whole lifetime.

pages.text: How Much Is a Million? We write one million as a one followed by six zeros, like this: 1,000,000. Do you know how much a million is? Some of the world’s largest cities have millions of people living in them. If you are lucky, you might win a million dollars in a lottery. Ten Largest Cities in the World.
pages.brief: A busy city skyline shows millions of residents living close together, while a lottery ticket and a small pile of dollar bills sit in the foreground, illustrating everyday examples of one million people and one million dollars.

pages.text: I’ve Told You a Million Times! Maybe you think your parents have told you to clean your room a million times. But have they really? Let’s say that every day your parents tell you ten times to clean your room. You would be over 273 years old before they told you for the millionth time!
pages.brief: A parent stands in a doorway pointing at a messy child’s bedroom while the child sits among toys, and a long calendar stretches past to suggest more than 273 years of repeated reminders to clean the room.

pages.text: A Million Pennies Imagine a jar with one thousand pennies in it. Now imagine one thousand jars, each with one thousand pennies inside.
pages.brief: A single glass jar filled with one thousand pennies stands in front, while rows and rows of identical penny-filled jars stretch far into the background, making a huge collection of one thousand jars each holding one thousand pennies.

pages.text: Ready or Not, Here I Come! Remember our earlier game of hide and seek? Let’s say you count to one million while your friends run and hide. You will count for over three weeks without stopping before you reach one million. Your friends will probably be very well hidden by then.
pages.brief: A child stands with eyes covered at a hide-and-seek base beside a tree, counting outdoors while friends dash away to hide; a long ribbon of day-and-night cycles suggests more than three weeks passing without stopping.

pages.text: How Much Is a Billion? We write one billion as a one followed by nine zeros, like this: 1,000,000,000. There are more than seven billion people alive on Earth right now. More than one billion of them are under the age of ten years old. That’s a lot of kids!
pages.brief: A view of Earth from space shows crowded continents filled with many people, and among them are more than one billion children under ten years old, suggesting the huge number of kids alive right now.

pages.text: But how much is a billion? Imagine I gave you a million dollars every day. At that rate, it would take almost two years and nine months before you had one billion dollars.
pages.brief: A person receives a fresh stack of a million dollars each day while a wall calendar fills with marked days, showing that daily gifts of a million dollars would take almost two years and nine months to reach one billion.

pages.text: How long do you think it would take to count to a billion during a game of hide and seek? If you counted that high, your game would last about one hundred years! And that’s if you didn’t stop to sleep, eat, drink, or do anything else while you counted.
pages.brief: A child counts at a hide-and-seek base while seasons change and years pass around the outdoor game, and the hidden friends wait so long that the whole game stretches about one hundred years without stopping.

pages.text: A Billion Pennies Remember the jar of one thousand pennies? Imagine stacking one billion pennies up in the shape of a block. The block would be about the size of five school buses.
pages.brief: A giant block made of one billion stacked pennies stands beside five school buses in a parking lot, showing its enormous size; the penny block is about as large as all five buses lined up together.

pages.text: How Much Is a Trillion? A billion is a big number, but a trillion is much larger. One thousand times larger to be exact. We write one trillion as a one followed by twelve zeros, like this: 1,000,000,000,000. But what does a trillion look like? Imagine that you stacked up one trillion pennies in the shape of a cube. Each side of the cube would be almost as long as a football field.
pages.brief: A gigantic cube built from one trillion stacked pennies rises beside a football field, with each side almost as long as the field itself, making the tremendous scale of a trillion clearly visible to viewers.

pages.text: Big Numbers Are Useful People who work in science, business, and government often use big numbers in their work. A scientist might use big numbers to measure the distance from Earth to the Sun. A businessperson might use them to count how many products a company has sold. A city planner might use them to decide how many schools a city with millions of people needs.
pages.brief: A scientist measures the distance from Earth to the Sun, a businessperson counts products a company has sold, and a city planner studies how many schools a city with millions of people needs, showing big numbers at work.

pages.text: Conclusion Knowing about millions, billions, and trillions can help us understand our world and our universe. So don’t be afraid of really big numbers and the words we use for them. Big numbers have a million uses!
pages.brief: A child looks up at a starry sky above a city skyline, with large simple number shapes woven into the scene, suggesting that millions, billions, and trillions help us understand our world and our universe.

books.title: Hermit Crabs
books.art_why: Hermit crabs and their beach and ocean habitats exist today, so photographs are suitable.

pages.text: Shell-Changing Night A hermit crab hurries across the beach. An empty shell just washed in. The shell is a little bigger than the one he’s been using. He grabs the new shell with his claws. Then he pokes his head inside. It’s empty. He stands on two legs. Then he slips his body out of his old shell and into the new one. He’s in!
pages.brief: On a beach at night, a hermit crab hurries across the sand toward an empty seashell that has just washed in. The new shell is a little bigger than his old one. He grips it with his claws, pokes his head inside, stands on two legs, and slips from the old shell into the new one.

pages.text: What Do Hermit Crabs Look Like? Hermit crabs are related to other crabs and also to lobsters and shrimp. A hermit crab has its own hard outer shell, called an exoskeleton. But the exoskeleton only covers part of its body. A hermit crab wears an old seashell to protect its soft parts.
pages.brief: A hermit crab is shown with a crab, a lobster, and a shrimp to show they are related. The crab’s hard outer exoskeleton covers only part of its body. It wears an old seashell over its soft parts for protection.

pages.text: A hermit crab has five pairs of legs. The first pair of legs ends in claws. The second and third pairs are for walking. The fourth and fifth pairs are short. The crab uses the little back legs to hold onto its shell home. A hermit crab also has two pairs of antennae. They help the crab taste water and find food. There are more than eight hundred different kinds of hermit crabs. Some are as tiny as a penny. Others are as big as a softball.
pages.brief: A hermit crab is shown from above with its five pairs of legs: claws in front, walking legs next, and short back legs holding its shell home. Two pairs of antennae reach out. Nearby, one tiny hermit crab is as small as a penny, and another is as big as a softball.

pages.text: How Do Hermit Crabs Live? Hermit crabs live in warm oceans all around the world. Some hermit crabs live on beaches or in tidal pools. Others live in the water. All hermit crabs are scavengers. They will eat just about any food they can find. Seaweed? Love it. Dead fish? They’re great. Rotting wood? Dinner is served.
pages.brief: In warm ocean water around the world, hermit crabs search for food. Some are on a beach or in a tidal pool, while others are underwater. One eats seaweed, another nibbles a dead fish, and another feeds on rotting wood.

pages.text: Hermit crabs are mostly nocturnal, which means they move around at night. They hide in their shells during the day. Baby Hermit Crabs Hermit crabs start as eggs. The eggs hatch in the water, and larvae (LAR-vee) float out. The larvae look like tiny shrimp. For a few months, they grow and change shape. When they are big enough, they find an empty seashell and join the colony.
pages.brief: At night, hermit crabs move around; during the day, they hide in their shells. In the water, eggs hatch into larvae that float like tiny shrimp. After months of growing and changing shape, a young crab finds an empty seashell and joins the colony.

pages.text: As young hermit crabs grow, their exoskeletons don’t get any bigger. So every year or so, they molt. They get rid of their old exoskeleton and grow a new one that’s the right size. Hermit crabs can live to be thirty years old, but most live six to ten years. Danger! Birds, octopuses, fish, and other animals will eat hermit crabs if they can. If a crab senses danger, it pulls into its shell and sits still.
pages.brief: A young hermit crab leaves its old exoskeleton behind and grows a new one that fits. Nearby, birds, an octopus, and a fish approach, so another crab pulls into its shell and sits still for safety.

pages.text: Not Really Hermits Hermit crabs got their name by mistake. Hermit crabs hide inside their shell “homes” when they are scared. People thought this meant they wanted to live alone, like hermits. But these crabs don’t like to live alone at all. They like to live in groups. Hermit Crabs: Not Easy Pets Many pet stores sell hermit crabs. But hermit crabs can be tricky to care for. The crabs need a moist area. They need to be calm. They need places to dig. And they need other crabs. Hermit crabs that don’t get the right care suffer and sometimes die. If you want to keep hermit crabs as pets, please learn to give them what they need to be healthy and happy.
pages.brief: A scared hermit crab hides inside its shell, while several other hermit crabs are in a pet store. They share a moist area with places to dig and stay close together in a group. They need calm care and other crabs to be healthy and happy.

pages.text: Watch Them Run! Hermit crabs look funny when they run across the sand. But they do more than make us smile. Hermit crabs have important jobs to do. They keep beaches clean by eating dead fish and plants. Seeing hermit crabs is usually a sign that a beach is healthy.
pages.brief: Hermit crabs run across the sand in a funny way. One eats a dead fish and plants, helping keep the beach clean. Several healthy hermit crabs on the beach are a sign that the beach is healthy, too.

books.title: Parrots
books.art_why: Parrots exist today and can be photographed.

pages.text: Special Birds There are many interesting birds in the world, and parrots are among the most amazing. What makes parrots so special?
pages.brief: Several parrots are shown among a variety of interesting birds in a lively outdoor scene, drawing attention as the most amazing ones. The parrots look active and unusual, while other birds fill the surrounding branches and greenery.

pages.text: Pretty Birds Many parrots are beautiful, with bright feathers in one or more bold colors. Parrots can be green, blue, yellow, red, or a mix of many colors. They can also be black, white, or gray. They can even be pink!
pages.brief: Many parrots perch together, their bright feathers showing bold colors. Some are green, blue, yellow, red, black, white, gray, or pink, and others have a mix of many colors. Their feathers look smooth and vivid in the sunlight.

pages.text: Smart Birds Parrots are super smart. Like humans, apes, and dolphins, parrots’ brains make up a big part of their bodies. Large brains give parrots the ability to learn, remember, and reason. Scientists have studied some parrots that are as smart as children in kindergarten.
pages.brief: A parrot stands with its large, round head prominent, showing the big brain that helps it learn, remember, and reason. A scientist watches nearby, studying the parrot. In the background, a human, an ape, and a dolphin appear together, all known for large brains.

pages.text: Talking Birds What parrots are best known for, however, is their ability to learn and mimic sounds. Many parrots can repeat words or sounds they hear. Some parrots can even speak using hundreds of different words. African grey parrots are famous for their speaking ability. Some African greys can tell jokes, count, and correctly name shapes and colors. Some of them can even speak in more than one language! Do You Know? Humans use vocal cords to talk, but parrots don’t have vocal cords. Parrots have to change the shape of the walls of their throats to speak.
pages.brief: An African grey parrot perches on a branch with its beak open, repeating sounds it has heard. Near it are a few colored shapes, showing the kinds of things some African greys can name. The scene focuses on the parrot's famous speaking ability.

pages.text: What Makes a Parrot a Parrot? There are more than 350 different kinds of parrots. The three main groups of parrots are true parrots, cockatoos, and New Zealand parrots. Although parrots come in many different shapes and sizes, they are all alike in some ways. What’s in a Name? Parrots include many different birds, such as: Amazon parrots, African parrots, macaws, parakeets (including budgerigars or “budgies”), parrotlets, conures, lories, lorikeets, lovebirds, cockatoos, cockatiels, kakas, kakapos, and keas.
pages.brief: Several parrots of different shapes and sizes stand together, including a cockatoo, a macaw, and a small budgerigar. They belong to the many kinds of parrots, such as true parrots, cockatoos, and New Zealand parrots. Their varied sizes show how different parrots can be.

pages.text: Parrot Beaks Almost all parrots have large, curved bills with a pointed upper half and a short, strong lower half. Parrots are sometimes called hookbills because their upper bills are shaped like hooks. Strong bills allow many parrots to crack open nuts and fruits that other animals can’t. Parrots also use their bills to hold objects, clean their feathers, and help them climb.
pages.brief: A close view of a parrot's head shows its large, curved bill with a pointed upper half and a short, strong lower half. The parrot grips a nut in its bill and cracks it open, while another parrot uses its bill to climb.

pages.text: Parrot Toes All parrots have four toes on each foot, with two toes pointing forward and two pointing backward. They use their feet for climbing, cleaning their heads and beaks, and grabbing and holding objects. They are the only birds that hold their food in one foot while they eat it. Do You Know? Because they have toes pointing both forward and backward, parrots are good at hanging upside down. Some parrots, known as hanging parrots, even sleep upside down!
pages.brief: A parrot hangs upside down from a branch, gripping it with four toes: two pointing forward and two pointing backward. In one foot, it holds a piece of food while eating. Another parrot uses its foot to clean its head and beak.

pages.text: Parrot Heads Parrots have large, round heads with eyes on the sides. Most have circles of skin around their eyes where there are no feathers. Some parrots have a crest, or crown, of feathers on the top of their heads. Cockatiels and cockatoos can raise and lower the feathers on their crests. They use their crests to communicate with other birds and to scare away predators.
pages.brief: A cockatoo raises the crest of feathers on top of its large, round head. Its eyes sit on the sides, with circles of bare skin around them. It faces another bird, using the raised crest to communicate.

pages.text: What Parrots Eat Parrots eat fruits, nuts, seeds, flowers, and other plant parts. Some also eat insects and other small creatures. A few kinds of parrots feed on nectar, a sugary liquid made by flowering plants. These parrots have special tongues that help them get nectar from flowers. Wowser! Parrots live a long time. Some larger parrots can live to be more than 85 years old!
pages.brief: A parrot holds a piece of fruit in its foot while eating. Nearby, another parrot reaches its special tongue into a flower to feed on nectar. Around them are nuts, seeds, flowers, and other plant parts, showing the foods parrots eat.

pages.text: Where Parrots Live Most parrots live in warm rainforests in tropical and subtropical areas. Central America, South America, and the islands in and around Australia have the greatest variety of parrots.
pages.brief: Several parrots perch among tall, leafy trees in a warm rainforest. The lush green setting suggests tropical and subtropical areas, where most parrots live. Many parrots gather in the trees, showing the great variety found in Central America, South America, and islands around Australia.

pages.text: Only a few kinds of parrots build nests. Most parrots live in hollow spaces that grow naturally in tree trunks. Some dig holes in cliffs, banks, or the ground. Do You Know? A parrot’s beak never stops growing. The beak is made of hard keratin, a much stronger version of what your fingernails are made of. Parrots need to eat hard, solid foods often to wear down their beaks so they don’t grow too large.
pages.brief: A parrot sits at the hollow opening in a tree trunk, while another digs a hole in a sandy bank. Nearby, a third parrot eats a hard, solid food, wearing down its ever-growing beak. Only a few kinds build nests, so most use hollow spaces like these.

pages.text: Parrots Are Popular Parrots are the rock stars of the bird world. Their beauty, intelligence, and playfulness have made them popular with people everywhere. Parrots As Pets Many people keep parrots as pets. Unfortunately, parrots can be hard to care for properly. Because they are very smart, parrots get bored easily, so they need a lot of attention. Parrots are loud and messy. They naturally want to fly and be with other birds.
pages.brief: A pet parrot perches in a home near a person who gives it attention. Scattered food shows it is messy, and its open beak suggests it is loud. Outside, other birds fly together, showing what the parrot naturally wants.

books.title: History of the Bicycle
books.art_why: The book covers 1800s bicycles and historical inventors, so drawn scenes fit best.

pages.text: Introduction People started building bicycles in the 1800s. Since then, bicycles have grown more and more popular. Today, more than one billion people around the world ride bicycles. The design of bicycles has changed over time. However, they still have two wheels and are a lot of fun!
pages.brief: In a sunny city park, many people of different ages ride two-wheeled bicycles along a path. Some smile and pedal side by side, showing how popular bicycles are around the world. The bikes have simple frames and two wheels, and everyone is having fun.

pages.text: Early Bicycles Karl Drais built the first bicycle in 1817. He called his invention the running machine. The frame and wheels were made of wood. It had no pedals. Instead, the rider pushed the bike along with their feet.
pages.brief: In an outdoor scene from 1817, Karl Drais stands beside his wooden running machine, a two-wheeled bicycle with a wooden frame and no pedals. He pushes the machine forward with his feet on the ground, demonstrating how the rider moved along.

pages.text: After that, inventors made many changes to the bicycle. Around 1840, the first pedals were added. The pedals turned the rear wheel with cranks. These were attached to long rods. Pedals kept the rider’s feet off the ground.
pages.brief: Around 1840, an inventor rides an early bicycle with pedals connected by long rods to cranks on the rear wheel. The rider’s feet rest on the pedals, lifted off the ground, while the rods and cranks turn the back wheel on a dirt road.

pages.text: During the 1860s, two French inventors made pedals that turned the front wheel. Their new bike had a heavy iron frame. Its tires were made of iron or wood.
pages.brief: In a French workshop during the 1860s, two inventors stand beside a heavy bicycle with an iron frame. Its pedals turn the front wheel, and its tires look hard, made of iron or wood. The inventors examine the new front-wheel pedal design.

pages.text: The Ordinary Built in 1871, the ordinary had a tall wheel in front and a small wheel in back. The rider sat on a seat above the front wheel.
pages.brief: An ordinary bicycle from 1871 stands outdoors with a tall front wheel and a small rear wheel. A rider sits high on a seat above the large front wheel, holding the handlebars, ready to move along a path.

pages.text: The ordinary moved faster than earlier bikes because of its large wheel. The big wheel also caused problems. It was hard to ride up a hill. It was also hard to get on and off the high seat. Riders often fell onto their heads when they tried to slow or stop the bike. These problems made this bike dangerous.
pages.brief: A rider struggles on a tall ordinary bicycle while climbing a hill, the large front wheel making the ride fast but difficult. Nearby, another rider has fallen forward onto his head after trying to slow down. The high seat and big wheel show why the ordinary was dangerous.

pages.text: The Safety Bicycle John Starley created the Rover safety bicycle in 1885. It looked like the bicycles of today. Most safety bicycles moved on two wheels of about the same size. A low seat between the wheels made the bike safer and easier to ride. The first safety bicycles had solid rubber tires. Later, these were changed to air-filled rubber tires. They made for a much less bumpy ride!
pages.brief: John Starley stands beside his Rover safety bicycle from 1885. It has two wheels of about the same size and a low seat between them. Nearby, a rider tries a version with air-filled rubber tires on a smoother road, showing the less bumpy ride.

pages.text: The safety bicycle used a gear and chain system. A chain connected gears on the back wheel to another gear. That gear was attached to the pedals. Riders pushed the pedals to turn the back wheel. Gears of different sizes made it easier to ride uphill, downhill, or on flat roads. Safety bicycles were less dangerous and more comfortable than earlier bikes. Because of this, more people began riding bicycles.
pages.brief: A rider pedals a safety bicycle on a road, with the chain and gears clearly visible. The chain connects the gear on the back wheel to the gear attached to the pedals. Different gear sizes help the rider handle an uphill slope, a downhill stretch, and flat ground.

pages.text: The Golden Age of the Bicycle In 1885, there were hundreds of bicycle factories in the United States. By 1900, over ten million people in the country owned bikes. Bicycles improved and became more popular. In 1889 Isaac Johnson, a Black American inventor, created a folding bicycle. In the 1890s, a Roadster bike was invented for women. This made it easy for women to get onto and ride their bicycles. It often came with a skirt guard. This stopped skirts and dresses from tangling in the rear wheel. These years became known as the Golden Age of the Bicycle. The Golden Age ended in the early 1900s. That is when factories started to produce inexpensive cars.
pages.brief: In a busy American street in the 1890s, many people ride bicycles past a bicycle factory. A Black inventor shows a folding bicycle. A woman rides a Roadster with a skirt guard over the rear wheel. An early car sits nearby, hinting at the Golden Age’s end.

pages.text: The Future of Bikes Today’s bikes have the same basic form as the safety bicycle. However, the design has changed many times. New materials make bikes stronger, faster, and lighter.
pages.brief: A sleek modern bicycle stands beside an older safety bicycle, showing the same basic two-wheel form. Riders test strong, fast, light bikes made with new materials on a smooth road. The frames look different from old designs but keep two wheels and pedals.

pages.text: The Bicycle: A Time Line.
pages.brief: A row of bicycles from different eras stands in order, from a wooden running machine pushed by feet to a tall ordinary, then a safety bicycle, and finally a modern bike. The bicycles are displayed outdoors on a clean surface, each one showing a different stage in design.

pages.text: Every year, people invent new ideas for bicycles. One inventor has designed a bike to ride over land and water. People make bicycles out of recycled materials like plastic, wood, and bamboo. Bikes will continue to change. Who knows what bikes of the future will look like?
pages.brief: An inventor rides a special bicycle from land into water, showing a bike designed for both. Nearby, other bicycles are built from recycled plastic, wood, and bamboo. More unusual future bike designs stand around, suggesting that bicycles will keep changing in surprising ways.

books.title: The Story of Rapa Nui
books.art_why: Much of the book shows historical events and early island life that cannot be photographed.

pages.text: The Story of Rapa Nui The Story of Rapa Nui Written by Cynthia Kennedy Henzel and Rachel Toliver.
pages.brief: A simple opening scene for the story of Rapa Nui shows the island as a broad, quiet place under a wide sky. The two authors, Cynthia Kennedy Henzel and Rachel Toliver, are shown as the book’s creators beside the island setting.

pages.text: Island of Mystery Deep in the South Pacific is a place called Rapa Nui. It is also known as Easter Island. The island is home to about six thousand people and hundreds of giant stone statues called moai. It is also home to many stories and legends.
pages.brief: A wide view of Rapa Nui, also called Easter Island, set deep in the South Pacific Ocean. About six thousand people and hundreds of giant stone moai statues are shown on the island, with stories and legends suggested by the mysterious landscape.

pages.text: Who Made the Moai? About nine hundred years ago, Polynesian people came to Rapa Nui. The island is very hard to get to. The nearest land is over a thousand miles away. The people made Rapa Nui their home and named a king. They are believed to have made the moai.
pages.brief: About nine hundred years ago, Polynesian people arrive at Rapa Nui after a long journey across a vast ocean, with no nearby land in sight. They settle on the island, name a king, and are shown as the people believed to have made the moai.

pages.text: Why Were the Moai Made? The 887 moai might have been made as symbols of power and religion. They might also have been made to remind people of their ancestors. Many moai are found near fresh drinking water. They are also found near places where people probably grew gardens. So, they might have been created to mark fresh water.
pages.brief: Many of the 887 moai stand as symbols of power and religion, and as reminders of ancestors. Some are near fresh drinking water and near places where people probably grew gardens, so the statues are shown marking fresh water and garden areas.

pages.text: Walking Statues? Scientists found a pit where the moai were cut from a stone wall. They also discovered the stone tools used to make the moai. However, scientists were still not sure how people moved the moai to the edge of the island.
pages.brief: Scientists examine a pit where moai were cut from a stone wall. Stone tools used to make the moai lie nearby. The scientists are shown studying the site, still unsure how people moved the moai to the edge of the island.

pages.text: Many moai are the size of two tall people. They are as heavy as a school bus. They are too heavy to drag around. The people of the island had no carts.
pages.brief: A moai stands beside two tall people to show its size. The statue is as heavy as a school bus, far too heavy to drag around, and the people of the island are shown with no carts to move it.

pages.text: Scientists wondered if tree trunks were used to roll the moai. But the Rapa Nui people living on the island today have stories and songs about walking statues. Could they be true?
pages.brief: Scientists imagine tree trunks being used to roll a moai, while Rapa Nui people living on the island today share stories and songs about walking statues. The scene shows the old tree-trunk idea beside the living stories, asking whether the walking statues could be true.

pages.text: A Rapa Nui scientist said yes! So, another group of scientists did some tests to see if moai could walk. They tied long ropes to the top of a moai. People pulled on the ropes. The statue rocked back and forth. The moai moved forward little by little as the people pulled. The moai was walking!
pages.brief: A Rapa Nui scientist agrees that moai could walk, so another group of scientists tests the idea. People tie long ropes to the top of a moai and pull. The statue rocks back and forth and moves forward little by little as the people pull, showing the moai walking.

pages.text: The Mysterious Past Some parts of the history of Rapa Nui are still mysterious. There may once have been as many as 10,000 people on the island. By 1877, only 111 people were left. There are different ideas about when people disappeared—and why.
pages.brief: The mysterious past of Rapa Nui is shown with a once-busy island that may have had as many as 10,000 people. By 1877, only 111 people are left. Different ideas about when people disappeared and why are suggested by the quiet, uncertain scene.

pages.text: One idea was that as people cut down the island’s many trees, the soil needed to grow crops washed away. This could have caused people to starve. Rats, which came to the island on the Rapa Nui people’s boats, also ate many nuts from the trees. This would cause fewer trees to grow. However, now scientists know the Rapa Nui people also had successful gardens. The trees were gone, but the people could still eat food from gardens.
pages.brief: One idea shows people cutting down the island’s many trees, soil washing away, and rats that came on boats eating nuts from the trees. Scientists now know the Rapa Nui people also had successful gardens, so even with the trees gone, people could still eat food from gardens.

pages.text: Some people disappeared because they were enslaved. In 1859, people came from Peru to Rapa Nui. They enslaved about 1,500 people from the island and took them away. People from other countries also brought sicknesses that caused people on Rapa Nui to die.
pages.brief: In 1859, people from Peru come to Rapa Nui and enslave about 1,500 people from the island, taking them away. People from other countries also bring sicknesses that cause people on Rapa Nui to die. The scene shows the taking away and the sickness.

pages.text: A year later, in 1860, island stories say that a civil war took place on Rapa Nui. Two groups, the Long-Ears and the Short-Ears, fought. Weapons discovered later by scientists support this story. Around the time of the war, some moai were pushed over. No one is sure why. Some think the moai were tipped face down to protest the war.
pages.brief: In 1860, island stories tell of a civil war between two groups, the Long-Ears and the Short-Ears. Weapons found later support the story. Around the time of the war, some moai are pushed over. Some people think the moai were tipped face down to protest the war.

pages.text: Rapa Nui Today Thousands of Rapa Nui people live on the island and in Chile today. Some of them study the moai. In 1989, Rapa Nui scientists discovered pieces of shells that turned out to be moai eyes. As time goes on, people will continue to discover more about the amazing moai and the people who created them.
pages.brief: Thousands of Rapa Nui people live on the island and in Chile today. Some of them study the moai. In 1989, Rapa Nui scientists discover pieces of shells that turn out to be moai eyes. The scene shows scientists examining the shell eyes as people continue to discover more about the moai and their creators.

books.title: Empire State Building
books.art_why: The Empire State Building, its builders and New York City all exist in the real world and are widely photographed.

pages.text: Two Friends Think Big Two friends, John Raskob and Al Smith, wanted to build the tallest skyscraper in the world. They grew up in low-income families. Both had to quit school and go to work. Years later, Raskob was rich and Smith was famous. Together, the two friends made a good team and built the Empire State Building. Their building was the tallest in the world for forty-one years.
pages.brief: Two men in suits, John Raskob and Al Smith, stand together outdoors with the tall grey Empire State Building rising behind them in New York City. A small imagined glimpse of their boyhood shows two schoolboys leaving their books to go to work in a shop and a factory.

pages.text: Stars and States Take an elevator to the top of this building, and you can see parts of five states. Look around and you might see stars, even in the daytime. Famous movie stars visit to see the view, too. View From the Empire State Building From the top of the Empire State Building, you can see five states.
pages.brief: Visitors lean on the railing of a high open-air observation deck on top of the Empire State Building, looking out over a wide city of rooftops, rivers and distant land. Above them in the pale daytime sky a few faint stars and a small airplane dot the blue.

pages.text: The Empire State Building From the ground to the top is 1,454 feet (443 m). The building has its own zip code—10118. The Empire State Building is known as the “world’s most famous office building,” “America’s favorite building,” and even one of the Seven Wonders of the Modern World. The 102nd floor is for visitors. The 86th floor is for visitors. The address is 350 Fifth Avenue, New York City. The ground floor is much larger than a football field.
pages.brief: The whole Empire State Building is shown from street level to its tower and spire against a clear sky, the ground floor spreading wider than a football field. Two small observation decks stand out high on the building, one at the 86th floor and one at the 102nd, with tiny visitors behind the railings.

pages.text: Making Room for Greatness The place Raskob and Smith chose for their building was a busy one. A grand hotel was already standing there. The hotel had to go. People worked day and night to tear down the hotel quickly. The two friends needed to construct their building fast.
pages.brief: A grand old hotel with ornate stone walls and many windows is being torn down in busy New York City. Workers with tools and machines pull at the walls day and night, dust rising, while crowds of people in coats and hats pass by on the crowded sidewalk in front.

pages.text: A skyscraper as big and heavy as the one they planned needed to sit on solid rock. Workers dug down 40 feet (12.2 m) to reach solid rock. Huge trucks carried away tons of dirt and rock. It took five months to tear down the hotel and make the hole. Then, on April 7, 1930, construction of the Empire State Building began.
pages.brief: Workers deep in a huge open pit dig down with shovels and machines to reach solid grey rock, the walls of the hole rising high above their heads. Nearby, big trucks loaded with tons of dirt and rock rumble away from the site as the foundation hole takes shape.

pages.text: Sky Boys Strong metal beams rose. Beams support the skyscraper much as your bones support your body. As the steel beams went higher and higher, crowds gathered on the streets below. They looked up in wonder as men walked the narrow beams high above. People called the men “sky boys.”
pages.brief: Tall steel beams climb into the sky over New York City while crowds of people fill the streets below, faces tipped up in wonder. High on the narrow beams, men in work clothes walk and balance, guiding the next pieces of steel into place.

pages.text: Do You Know? Many proud and brave ironworkers were from the Mohawk Nation, Native people who lived in or near New York. More than 800 Mohawk lived in a neighborhood called Downtown Kahnawake (gah-nah-WAH-geh). A sign over the doorway of a restaurant there said, “The Greatest Ironworkers in the World Pass Through These Doors.” Sky boys worked in teams of four to join the beams together with red-hot rivets. Every team member was brave and fast. The steel beams zoomed up an amazing four floors a week. Some of the best teams were the Mohawk from New York State. Some of them could set a rivet every minute.
pages.brief: A team of four ironworkers, several of them Mohawk men, work high on the steel frame catching a glowing red-hot rivet and hammering it into a beam. Below them in a New York neighbourhood, families walk past brick buildings and a busy restaurant doorway.

pages.text: Zoom to the Top By June, the steel reached the 25th floor. Behind the sky boys came other workers. They built the outside wall of the building. These workers were so fast that they started to catch up to the sky boys.
pages.brief: The steel skeleton of the Empire State Building has climbed to the 25th floor, beams crisscrossing against the sky. Just below and behind the steelworkers, other workers in caps and overalls bolt stone, window frames and metal onto the outside of the rising floors.

pages.text: August was the busiest month. The sky boys were almost to the top. The outside wall made of stone, windows, and metal was going up a floor a day. Inside, thousands of workers were busy.
pages.brief: High above New York City the sky boys work near the top of the steel frame while the outside wall of pale stone, glass windows and metal rises a floor a day. Inside the lower floors, thousands of workers swarm over beams and tools, busy in every direction.

pages.text: Getting supplies to so many workers was taking too much time. Workers laid tracks around each floor to speed things up. Carts were loaded and pushed along the tracks right to the workers.
pages.brief: Inside a bare floor of the half-built skyscraper, workers lay narrow tracks across the concrete and push loaded carts along them. Stacks of supplies and tools sit in piles, and workers reach out to take materials from the carts as they arrive.

pages.text: In November, Al Smith stood proud. He was on the 102nd floor. The steel beams had reached the very top. He was also scared standing that high up on a beam. The last rivet was placed. When he smashed it into the beam, the steel work was done! That rivet made newspaper headlines. Not only was it the last one set, but it was also the only one made of gold.
pages.brief: Al Smith stands high on the 102nd floor, holding a rivet hammer, his face proud and a little scared as he looks down. He smashes a shining gold rivet into the last steel beam, and reporters below lift cameras as the steelwork is finished.

pages.text: Happy Birthday! The building opened on May 1, 1931. Fifty years later, in 1981, the building was made a landmark. It is protected by law and cannot be torn down. Al Smith said his building was made for the future, and he was right! It will be standing tall in New York for a long time to come.
pages.brief: A crowd gathers on a New York street in spring sunshine as the finished Empire State Building towers above them, its limestone walls and spire complete. Visitors stream through the doors and people look up, glad the landmark will stand tall for the future.

books.title: Incredible Places to Stay
books.art_why: All the hotels are real places that exist today and can be photographed.

pages.text: Incredible Places to Stay.
pages.brief: A bright travel montage showing the six real hotels from the book side by side: a glass capsule on a cliff, an ice building, giraffes at a window, tree houses in a forest, a mine entrance and an underwater lodge. No people are shown, just the remarkable places waiting to be visited.

pages.text: World Map of Incredible Hotels 3 INDIAN OCEAN 5 Sala Silvermine Hotel, Sala, Sweden 1 Skylodge Adventure Suites, Cuzco, Peru 6 Jules’ Undersea Lodge, Key Largo, Florida 2 Hôtel de Glace, Quebec, Canada 7 Tundra Lodge, Manitoba, Canada 3 Giraffe Manor, Nairobi, Kenya 4 Treehotel, Harads, Sweden Introduction Get ready to go on a tour of some of the world’s most amazing hotels. You’ll swim to the bottom of the sea, sleep in a cave, and meet different animals. Pack your bags and let’s go!
pages.brief: A large world map across the page shows the continents, with small photographs of the seven hotels placed on their countries: Sweden, Peru, Canada, Kenya and Florida. The map gives a wide view of how far apart these unusual places are around the world.

pages.text: Sky High The first stop on your tour is Skylodge Adventure Suites in the Sacred Valley of Cuzco, Peru. You can sleep and eat in see-through capsules hanging high above the valley floor. Each capsule is solar powered and has a view of Sacred Valley. You’ll feel just like you’re in a giant bird nest!
pages.brief: Three see-through capsules hang high above the green Sacred Valley floor in Cuzco, Peru. Solar panels sit on the capsules and beds and a table are visible inside the clear walls. The pods look like a giant bird nest stuck to the steep rock face.

pages.text: A Cool Place to Stay The next stop on your tour is the Hôtel de Glace (O-tel DEH GLAHS) located outside of Quebec City, Canada. How cool is it? It’s a work of art made of ice! The rooms, halls, and most of the furniture are carved out of ice. It all melts away in the warm weather. Artists and workers spend about forty days every winter building it.
pages.brief: Outside Quebec City in Canada, a whole hotel is carved from ice and snow. Artists and workers in winter clothes shape the rooms, halls and furniture out of ice blocks with tools, snow heaped around them and cold blue light glowing through the carved walls.

pages.text: You’ll need to wear your heavy winter clothes during your stay. It’s as cold as a freezer in there! You’ll sleep in a special sleeping bag because the beds are made out of ice.
pages.brief: Inside the ice hotel, a guest in heavy winter clothes, hat and gloves climbs into a thick special sleeping bag. The bed frame and the room around it are carved from ice, with a frozen-looking bedside table and cold blue-white walls shining faintly.

pages.text: Breakfast with Giraffes From Canada, you’ll travel to Giraffe Manor in Kenya. The forests around the hotel are home to some of the tallest giraffes in the world.
pages.brief: Giraffe Manor in Kenya stands among green forests, and some of the world's tallest giraffes stand tall among the trees nearby, their long necks reaching up to the leaves. The hotel building sits peacefully in the warm African landscape.

pages.text: Every morning, the giraffes leave the forest for the hotel. They stick their heads through open windows and doors. Guests feed breakfast to the giraffes. Profits made by the hotel support endangered animals.
pages.brief: Early in the morning, giraffes walk from the forest to the hotel and push their long necks and heads through open windows and doorways. Guests sit at a breakfast table holding out food, and the giraffes stretch down to take it from their hands.

pages.text: In the Trees The next stop on your tour is Sweden. There you’ll find the Treehotel: a hotel made up of strange tree houses. Six tree-house rooms hang 14 to 20 feet (4 to 6 m) off the ground. One room, the Mirrorcube, is covered with glass. This tree house blends in with the woods.
pages.brief: Six strange tree-house rooms hang fourteen to twenty feet above the ground in a Swedish wood. One room, the Mirrorcube, is covered in glass, so its mirrored walls reflect the surrounding trees and branches and it seems to vanish into the forest.

pages.text: Branches around the Bird’s Nest tree house make it look like the home of a giant bird. Another tree house looks like a UFO from outer space.
pages.brief: Two odd tree houses stand among tall Swedish trees. One is covered in branches that make it look like a giant bird's nest, while the other is shaped like a shiny flying saucer from outer space, resting high on a slender trunk.

pages.text: While you’re in Sweden, it is only a short drive to the deepest hotel room in the world. The Sala Silvermine Hotel sits on top of an old silver mine. Most of the rooms in the hotel are near the mine’s opening. You can also spend a night hundreds of feet underground in the Mine Suite. It is located more than 500 feet (152 m) beneath the surface. Dress in warm clothes. The temperature in the mine is only about 28°F (–2°C). However, the room is warmed to 64°F (18°C).
pages.brief: The Sala Silvermine Hotel sits above an old silver mine in Sweden. Most rooms are near the mine opening, while far below, hundreds of feet underground, a warmly lit Mine Suite is carved into dark rock, reached by a deep shaft, with visitors dressed in warm clothes.

pages.text: Sleeping with Fish The last stop on your tour is Jules’ Undersea Lodge in the Florida Keys. Be prepared to get wet! The lodge is 21 feet (6 m) underwater. You’ll need scuba gear to get to your room. Scuba Time The hotel offers a beginners’ scuba program for divers over ten years old. If you are under ten years old, you can still snorkel on the surface of the water and come back when you are older.
pages.brief: Jules' Undersea Lodge rests twenty-one feet below the surface in the Florida Keys, its windows glowing in the blue water. A diver in scuba gear swims down towards the entrance, while a younger snorkeler floats on the surface above, looking down.

pages.text: For dinner, you can even order pizza. Someone from the hotel will swim it down to you in a watertight box!
pages.brief: Underwater inside the lodge, a guest waits while someone from the hotel swims down through the water carrying a pizza sealed inside a watertight box. Bubbles rise past the swimmer as the food is delivered to the flooded entrance.

pages.text: Conclusion From the forests of Kenya to the bottom of the sea, amazing hotels are everywhere. These incredible places to stay offer you far more than just a bed for the night. They offer you an experience that you’ll never forget! Polar Bear Fun Tundra Lodge in Manitoba, Canada, looks like a train on huge wheels. The hotel moves over snow so that guests can get very close to polar bears.
pages.brief: The Tundra Lodge in Manitoba, Canada, looks like a train sitting on huge wheels, parked on a wide snowy plain. Out on the snow, polar bears wander close to the strange train-like building, and guests look out at them through the windows.

books.title: Inside Your Body
books.art_why: The human body and its systems are real, present-day subjects that can be shown realistically.

pages.text: The human body is an amazing machine. It has many parts that form systems. The systems work together to keep you alive and healthy. Let’s look at some of your body’s systems. Introduction.
pages.brief: A full human figure stands in a clear science view, showing a healthy body made of many parts that form systems. The body’s systems are shown working together inside the figure to keep it alive and healthy.

pages.text: Skeletal System There are 206 bones in your body that make up your skeleton. Your bones give your body shape and strength. They also protect your inner organs. Most of the bones in your body are linked together at joints. There are different kinds of joints. Different joints let body parts move in different ways. The joint that joins your arm and shoulder lets your arm rotate. The joints at your elbows and knees let your lower arms and legs move up and down. If it were not for moving joints, you could not walk, run, and swim.
pages.brief: A human skeleton is shown from head to toe in a clear science view, with bones giving the body shape and strength and guarding inner organs. The arm rotates at the shoulder joint, while the elbow and knee joints let the lower arm and leg move up and down. The skeleton stands in a walking pose.

pages.text: Muscular System Muscles control the movement of your body. There are three kinds of muscles. Skeletal muscle is the muscle that is attached to bones. It makes your arms, legs, fingers, eyes, and other body parts move. Cardiac muscle is the strong heart muscle. It works around the clock. Smooth muscle is found in your skin, stomach, and other organs. The brain tells muscles what to do. If your fingers go near something hot, a signal goes to the brain. It then sends a signal to tell your hand to move away. Your brain and thousands of miles of nerve fibers form your body’s communication system. The brain is the control center. It receives information from your sense organs—eyes, nose, ears, tongue, and skin. Nervous System.
pages.brief: A human figure shows skeletal muscles on arms, legs, fingers and eyes, cardiac muscle in the heart, and smooth muscle in skin and stomach. The brain and long nerve fibers connect to sense organs. One hand pulls away from something hot after a signal reaches the brain.

pages.text: The brain controls many functions of your body without your thinking about them. You breathe, your heart beats, and you digest food without thinking. It just happens. For other things, the brain tells muscles what to do. The brain decides what to do based on information from your sense organs. What it does depends a lot on what you have been taught. If you see the problem 2 + 2 =?, you know the answer because you were taught how to add. This system takes care of breathing. Oxygen is part of the air that you breathe. Air enters through your nose and mouth. It travels to your lungs through your trachea, or windpipe. Once air is in your lungs, blood removes the oxygen and takes it to the cells of your body. Your lungs also remove carbon dioxide from blood. The carbon dioxide leaves your body every time you breathe out. Respiratory System.
pages.brief: A human head and torso show the brain as control center, with lungs and windpipe below. Air enters through nose and mouth and travels down the trachea to the lungs, where blood takes oxygen and carbon dioxide leaves. The heart beats and food digests automatically.

pages.text: Circulatory System The circulatory system is made up of your heart and blood vessels. Your heart pumps blood through your body. It never rests. Blood delivers food and oxygen to every cell in your body. It also picks up waste products from cells and takes them to the lungs and kidneys. The waste then leaves your body. Digestion breaks down the food you eat. Food must be broken into very tiny particles so that it can be carried by the blood to cells. When food enters your mouth, it mixes with saliva, or spit. Saliva begins digesting the food. When you swallow, food travels down a long tube to your stomach, where it mixes with other chemicals that digest it more. Digestive System.
pages.brief: A human torso shows the heart pumping blood through vessels that carry food and oxygen to cells and take waste to lungs and kidneys. Above, food in the mouth mixes with saliva, then travels down a long tube to the stomach, where it mixes with digestive chemicals.

pages.text: Then the food enters your small intestine. Here, more chemicals mix with the food. Blood moving through the walls of the small intestine carries away the digested food. Food that is not digested continues on to your large intestine. It is then removed as waste. Humans must reproduce in order to survive. Special organs and glands in the reproductive system allow humans to make new human beings. Reproductive System.
pages.brief: A human digestive system shows food moving into the small intestine, where more chemicals mix with it and blood in the walls carries digested food away. Undigested food travels to the large intestine and leaves the body as waste. Nearby, reproductive organs and glands allow humans to make new human beings.

pages.text: Conclusion This is a look at some important systems in your body. Many other parts also help you stay strong and healthy. You can help your body do its job by eating well and getting exercise. You can also help by avoiding stress and unsafe situations. smooth muscle, 7 small intestine, 13 skeletal muscle, 7 sense organs, 8 large intestine, 13 cardiac muscle, 7 Index.
pages.brief: A healthy child stands in a bright everyday setting, with a strong, well body. Around the child, a simple meal, an exercise scene, and a calm safe place show eating well, getting exercise, and avoiding stress and unsafe situations.

books.title: Ocean Animals
books.art_why: Ocean animals exist today and can be photographed.

pages.text: Many kinds of animals live in the ocean and form an ocean community. Some ocean animals spend all their time in the water, but others spend some time on land. Let’s meet some of these ocean animals. Most of the animals in this book are mammals, fish, or reptiles.
pages.brief: A broad ocean scene shows many kinds of ocean animals forming a community: some swimming fully underwater, others spending time on land, including mammals, fish and reptiles.

pages.text: As a dolphin, my sleek body and strong tail help me swim fast. I live with other dolphins in a group called a pod. We whistle, click, and squeak to talk to each other. I swim to the surface a few times a minute to breathe. My brain is large, so people think I’m pretty smart. I like to eat fish. Like all walruses, I live on ice and in cold water. A thick layer of fat keeps me warm. My ivory tusks are long teeth that I use to dig for clams, protect myself, and move around. My flat flippers allow me to swim and move around on land. I make loud snorts and barks to talk to other walruses.
pages.brief: A sleek dolphin with a strong tail swims fast with its pod, whistling, clicking and squeaking, rising to the surface to breathe and eating fish. A walrus is on ice in cold water, kept warm by thick fat, with long ivory tusks to dig for clams and flat flippers for swimming and moving on land, and it snorts and barks.

pages.text: I am a hammerhead shark. The shape of my head gives me my name. Because my eyes are at the ends of two lobes, I can easily find prey. I use my large head to pin stingrays, my favorite food, to the ocean floor. During the day, I travel with other sharks, but I hunt alone at night. Known for barking like a dog, I am a California sea lion. People think I’m noisy and playful, but I’m also smart. My flippers and short fur help me swim fast. I can stay underwater for ten minutes. I live with other sea lions on rocky coasts. I eat squid, octopus, and fish.
pages.brief: A hammerhead shark with its wide, hammer-shaped head and eyes at the ends of two lobes swims with other sharks by day, then hunts alone at night, pinning a stingray to the ocean floor. A California sea lion barks like a dog on a rocky coast, using flippers and short fur to swim fast and stay underwater for ten minutes.

pages.text: I have a soft body and eight arms covered with suckers. I’m an octopus. I don’t have a skeleton, so I can fit into very small spaces. If I lose an arm, it will grow back. By shooting black ink and changing my skin color, I can hide in the ocean. I’m a great white shark, and I’m large and fierce. No other ocean animal hunts me. If I lose or break any of my three thousand sharp teeth, they’ll grow back. I hunt seals, dolphin, and fish. I can sense blood in water from far away.
pages.brief: A soft-bodied octopus with eight sucker-covered arms squeezes into a very small space, shoots black ink and changes skin color to hide in the ocean. A large, fierce great white shark with three thousand sharp teeth swims nearby; it hunts seals, dolphins and fish and can sense blood in the water from far away.

pages.text: Because my brain is bigger than any other fish’s brain, I’m smart— like all manta rays. My body is huge, flat, and wide. My fins look like wings. Although I’m related to stingrays, I don’t sting. I’m a sea horse, but I’m not a horse—I’m a fish! I use my snout to eat food such as shrimp. If I sense trouble, I change my color and shape. Male sea horses, not females, carry eggs in a pouch until they hatch.
pages.brief: A huge, flat, wide manta ray glides with fins like wings; its brain is bigger than any other fish’s, and although related to stingrays, it does not sting. A sea horse, a fish not a horse, uses its snout to eat shrimp, changes color and shape if it senses trouble, and the male carries eggs in a pouch.

pages.text: I have leathery skin instead of a shell, unlike other turtles. I’m a leatherback turtle—the biggest turtle in the world. I lay eggs on land by digging in the sand to make a nest. Diving deep in the ocean, I can stay underwater for longer than one hour. Jellyfish are my favorite food. I’m a blue whale, the largest mammal ever to live. My huge tongue weighs as much as an elephant! I make deep sounds that move through water. I eat small animals called krill by swallowing large amounts of water. I push the water out through brushlike teeth called baleen. The baleen traps my food inside my mouth.
pages.brief: A leatherback turtle with leathery skin instead of a shell, the biggest turtle, digs a nest in the sand to lay eggs, dives deep and stays underwater over an hour, eating jellyfish. A blue whale, the largest mammal ever, makes deep sounds through the water and swallows krill, pushing water out through baleen.

pages.text: All these animals live in the ocean. Pollution and hunting harm them, causing many to become endangered. By keeping our oceans clean, we can keep these animals alive. reptiles (n.) page 4 cold-blooded animals that are covered with scales or horny plates prey (n.) page 7 animals that are hunted and eaten pollution (n.) page 15 the act or result of putting harmful materials into the air, water, or soil mammals (n.) page 4 warm-blooded animals with hair or fur lobes (n.) page 7 rounded or curved sections of bodies or organs endangered (adj.) page 15 in danger of dying out completely Glossary.
pages.brief: All these ocean animals are together in the ocean, with harmful pollution and hunting shown as dangers that make many endangered. A clean ocean scene suggests keeping the water clean so the animals can stay alive.

books.title: Endangered Birds
books.art_why: The book covers the extinct great auk and historical hunting scenes, so drawings suit the mixed past and present bird stories.

pages.text: Introduction Have you ever seen a great auk (AWK)? These penguin-like birds once lived along the coasts from Iceland to Florida. But the great auk was fiercely hunted for its feathers and eggs. The very last ones were killed in 1844. Today, great auks are extinct. You can only see them in pictures, or see their skeletons in a museum.
pages.brief: A great auk, a penguin-like bird, stands on a rocky coastline near cold sea. Nearby, a museum shows a great auk skeleton. The living birds were hunted for feathers and eggs, and the last ones were killed in 1844, so great auks are extinct.

pages.text: There are many other birds that are endangered, or close to becoming extinct. We will look at some of those birds in this book. We will also see some ways that humans are trying to save them.
pages.brief: Several endangered birds are shown together, with people working nearby to protect them. The scene suggests that many other birds are close to extinction and that humans are trying some ways to save them.

pages.text: The Kakapo The kakapo (ka-ku-po) of New Zealand is one of the strangest, and rarest, birds in the world. It has short wings and cannot fly, but it has strong legs to walk through the mountains. It looks like an owl, and it comes out at night like an owl. But the kakapo is actually a parrot. Male kakapos make a booming call that sounds like a giant heartbeat.
pages.brief: At night in the mountains of New Zealand, a kakapo parrot stands on strong legs. It has short wings and an owl-like face. A male kakapo puffs out its chest and makes a deep booming call that sounds like a giant heartbeat.

pages.text: Before Europeans came to New Zealand, there were few predators, or meat-eating animals, on the islands. Europeans brought cats, rats, and dogs to New Zealand. The kakapos had never seen these animals, so they didn’t know how to defend themselves. And they couldn’t fly to escape. The predators killed so many birds that by the 1950s, the kakapo disappeared.
pages.brief: On a New Zealand island, cats, rats, and dogs move among the trees while kakapos stand on the ground. The kakapos have short wings and cannot fly away; they look confused as the predators approach. By the 1950s, no kakapos are left.

pages.text: Then, in 1974, a few males were found. But because there were no females to lay eggs, kakapos would become extinct once the males died. In 1980, four females were found. Humans moved the kakapos to small islands without predators. Scientists began breeding the kakapos, or helping them reproduce. Today, there are 62 kakapos.
pages.brief: On a small island without predators, people move kakapos from one place to another. Scientists watch the birds and help them breed. A few males were found in 1974, then four females in 1980; today there are 62 kakapos.

pages.text: Short-tailed albatross The Short-Tailed Albatross There were once millions of short- tailed albatrosses. These beautiful gull-like birds spend many years at sea before nesting. All the short-tailed albatrosses nested on a few islands around Japan.
pages.brief: A huge flock of short-tailed albatrosses, gull-like seabirds, glides over the ocean near Japan. Others gather to nest on a few small islands. They spend many years at sea before returning to these islands to nest.

pages.text: About one hundred years ago, women loved to wear feathers in their hats. Hunters killed thousands of albatrosses for their feathers. Soon, there were none left on the islands. It seemed that the short-tailed albatross was extinct.
pages.brief: About one hundred years ago, women wear hats decorated with long feathers. Hunters on a Japanese island kill thousands of short-tailed albatrosses and take their feathers. Soon no albatrosses are left nesting on the islands, and the birds seem extinct.

pages.text: Years after the last albatross was seen, a few were spotted nesting on a volcanic island. These albatrosses had been at sea while the others were killed. They were the last short-tailed albatrosses alive. Today, the albatrosses’ island is protected. The birds are still in danger, though. The volcanic island might erupt, killing the last short-tailed albatrosses.
pages.brief: A few short-tailed albatrosses nest on a volcanic island, with a smoking volcano behind them. These birds had been at sea while the others were killed. The island is now protected, but the volcano might erupt and kill the last albatrosses.

pages.text: The California Condor The California condor is the largest flying bird in North America. For many years, farmers, ranchers, and hunters shot and poisoned these birds. Do You Know? California condors often die of lead poisoning. A condor eats dead animals, some of which have been shot. The condor swallows the lead bullets with the meat. The condor’s strong stomach absorbs the poisonous lead, making the condor sick.
pages.brief: A California condor, the largest flying bird in North America, stands beside the body of a dead animal. It swallows pieces of meat containing lead bullets. Its strong stomach absorbs the poisonous lead, and the condor becomes sick. Farmers, ranchers, and hunters have shot and poisoned condors.

pages.text: In the 1980s, the last 27 living condors were caught. Now scientists take condor eggs and keep them warm until they hatch. Then, they hand-feed the chicks using condor puppets.
