The puppets help the chicks learn to live with other condors, instead of with humans. Once the chicks can fly, they are released into the wild.
pages.brief: Scientists catch the last 27 California condors. In a warm nursery, they keep condor eggs until they hatch. Then they use condor puppets to hand-feed the chicks, helping them learn to live with other condors instead of humans. Once the chicks can fly, they are released into the wild.

pages.text: The condors are still in danger after they are released. Some are shot. Others die by hitting power lines. Scientists still keep condors in zoos and raise chicks by hand. Someday all the condors may fly free.
pages.brief: A released California condor flies near power lines, while another condor stands in a zoo enclosure with scientists raising a chick by hand. Some condors are shot, and others die after hitting power lines. Scientists still keep condors in zoos and hope that someday all the condors fly free.

pages.text: Conclusion There are many other endangered birds in the world. Most are dying out because of human activity. But people are now trying to save these rare and beautiful animals from extinction.
pages.brief: Many different endangered birds are shown together, including rare and beautiful species. People work to protect them and their habitats. Most of these birds are dying out because of human activity, but people are now trying to save them from extinction.

books.title: Art Around Us
books.art_why: The book shows present-day artists and real art forms that can be photographed.

pages.text: Introduction Art is all around us. Art is in every shape, size, and color. Artists can make art from anything. Some artists make art with paint or paper. Others use glass or clay. Some use a computer. Others make art out of plants or sand.
pages.brief: A bright collection of art in many shapes, sizes, and colors shows artists using paint, paper, glass, clay, a computer, plants, and sand, making clear that art can be made from anything and is all around us.

pages.text: Painter Some artists are painters. Most painters use a brush. Others like to splash or spray paint. Some like to drip paint instead. It’s all painting.
pages.brief: A painter uses a brush on a painting as they work, while other painters splash, spray, or drip paint onto their work, showing different ways to paint and that all of these methods are painting.

pages.text: Painters paint on many surfaces. Most paint on canvas. Some paint on dishes or furniture. Have you seen a painted mural? A mural is big. It’s painted right on a wall.
pages.brief: Painters paint on many surfaces: most paint on canvas, some on dishes or furniture, and a mural painter covers a big wall right where it stands, showing paintings on everyday objects and large walls too.

pages.text: Sculptor Sculptors carve shapes with sharp tools. They might carve wood, stone, or ice. Other artists make soft sculpture. Soft sculptures are shapes made from fabric and yarn.
pages.brief: A sculptor carves shapes with sharp tools from wood, stone, or ice, while other artists make soft sculpture shapes from fabric and yarn, showing hard carving and soft fabric art side by side as they work.

pages.text: Some sculptors shape metal. They pour hot metal into a mold and let it cool. When they take the sculpture out, it’s shaped like the mold.
pages.brief: A sculptor shapes metal by pouring hot metal into a mold and letting it cool, then taking out the cooled sculpture so it has the shape of the mold, with heat and metalwork as the focus.

pages.text: Potter Potters make art with clay. They use their hands to shape the clay. Potters push on the clay. They pinch it. They pull it. They make it into the shape they want.
pages.brief: A potter uses hands to shape clay, pushing, pinching, and pulling it into the shape they want, with soft clay and hands alone forming the clay, showing how potters make art as they work with care.

pages.text: The clay shape is baked in a very hot oven. The heat bakes the clay until it’s dry. Baked clay is called ceramic. Potters use a special ceramic paint called a glaze. The glaze makes the ceramic shiny.
pages.brief: A potter’s clay shape is baked in a very hot oven until dry, becoming ceramic; then the potter adds a special ceramic paint called glaze that makes the finished ceramic shiny, with the hot oven and shiny glaze as the focus.

pages.text: Glassblower Melted glass is soft, like very thick glue. A glassblower scoops up a blob of hot, soft glass with the end of a long metal pipe. The pipe is hollow, like a straw. The artist blows air through the pipe into the blob of glass. The air makes a bubble in the glass. Then the glassblower can shape the bubble. He or she can make it wide, like a bowl, or make it flat, like a plate.
pages.brief: A glassblower scoops a blob of hot, soft glass onto the end of a long hollow metal pipe, blows air through the pipe to make a bubble, and shapes the bubble wide like a bowl or flat like a plate.

pages.text: Glassblowers work very quickly. While the glass is soft, they can change it. They can add dots or color. They can add a handle. But they have to be careful. When glass cools, it gets hard, and it can break easily.
pages.brief: Glassblowers work very quickly while the glass is soft, adding dots, color, or a handle, but they must be careful because cooling glass gets hard and can break easily, with the changing glass as the focus.

pages.text: Fiber Artist Art can be made with thread, yarn, and pieces of fabric. It’s called fiber art. Some fiber artists sew. Some make a quilt for a bed.
pages.brief: Fiber artists make art with thread, yarn, and pieces of fabric; some sew, and some make a quilt for a bed, showing colorful cloth, stitches, and soft materials coming together as warm handmade fiber art.

pages.text: Weavers are also fiber artists. Weavers loop yarns together to make art. They use a machine called a loom. The loom helps them put the yarns in the right place. Weavers can make beautiful rugs or blankets. They can weave a soft sculpture to hang on a wall.
pages.brief: Weavers loop yarns together to make art on a machine called a loom, which helps place the yarns, and they can make beautiful rugs or blankets or weave a soft sculpture to hang on a wall.

pages.text: Unusual Art Some art just looks different to us. It isn’t a painting. It isn’t a glass bowl. It’s hard to say what it is. Artists make it from things they found. Maybe they use pieces of wood and old junk. They might use parts of old toys, too. Some artists make big sculptures with sand. They get to work at the beach all day!
pages.brief: Unusual art looks different, hard to name, and is made from found things like pieces of wood, old junk, or parts of old toys; some artists also make big sculptures with sand at the beach all day.

pages.text: Many artists like to work outside. They make art in a park or a garden. They use tree branches, rocks, and plants to make a design. People can come to the park to see it.
pages.brief: Many artists work outside in a park or garden, using tree branches, rocks, and plants to make a design, and people come to the park to see the outdoor art set among nature around them.

pages.text: An art installation is big. It can be a whole room that is a work of art. Sometimes, you can walk around inside it. The artist fills the room with things to look at, touch, and hear. The room might have flashing lights or big video screens. You might hear music or strange sounds. You might smell flowers or popcorn.
pages.brief: An art installation is a whole room as a work of art; visitors can walk around inside it and see things to look at, touch, and hear, with flashing lights, big video screens, music, strange sounds, or smells like flowers or popcorn.

pages.text: Where Art Is Found Simple drawings are the oldest art in the world. Some very old drawings are on the walls of caves. Other old drawings were scratched into rocks. The drawings tell stories about something that had happened long ago. Art is also found in the ruins of very old cities. Scientists sometimes find old pottery designs. Some ruins have old murals painted on the walls.
pages.brief: Simple drawings are the oldest art, found on cave walls and scratched into rocks, telling stories about long-ago events; art is also found in ruins of very old cities, with old pottery designs and murals painted on walls.

pages.text: Art is everywhere. Explore your town to find types of art. Visit an art museum. You will see many types of painting and sculpture. Go to an art gallery or an art fair. Artists want you to see and enjoy what they make.
pages.brief: Art is everywhere, so people can explore a town, visit an art museum to see many types of painting and sculpture, or go to an art gallery or art fair where artists want everyone to see and enjoy what they make.

pages.text: Look for art around you. You can look for art when you are riding in a car. You might see a sculpture in a park. You might see a big mural on a wall.
pages.brief: People look for art around them while riding in a car, spotting a sculpture in a park or a big mural on a wall, showing that art can be found in everyday places nearby during a drive.

pages.text: You can make your own art. Draw on a sidewalk with chalk. Make a sculpture with clay, snow, or sand. Glue pieces of seashells, glass, and wood on a picture frame. It’s all art!
pages.brief: A child makes original art by drawing on a sidewalk with chalk, sculpting with clay, snow, or sand, and gluing seashells, glass, and wood onto a picture frame, showing that everyday materials can become art.

pages.text: You can tell a story with art. It can help you say how you feel. Art can be interesting or funny. It can be something that you just like to look at. Look for art. You’ll find it all around you!
pages.brief: A child tells a story with art and uses it to show how they feel, making art that is interesting, funny, or simply nice to look at, then looking for art and finding it all around them.

books.title: Solids All Around
books.art_why: The book uses instructional diagrams of geometric solids rather than photographs.

pages.text: Ruben and his friends are learning about solid figures all around them.
pages.brief: Ruben and several friends sit together in a classroom, looking at solid figures arranged around them. The children appear curious and attentive as they learn about rectangular prisms, cubes, spheres, cylinders, cones, and pyramids in the world around them.

pages.text: Rectangular Prisms This solid is a rectangular prism. You can see three of its faces. But there are three more faces that you can’t see. Every rectangular prism has six flat faces. The faces at the top and bottom of this prism are called bases. Both bases are the same size and shape. The bases are also opposite each other.
pages.brief: A single rectangular prism stands alone, showing three of its faces. The top and bottom faces are bases of the same size and shape, lying opposite each other, while three more faces remain hidden from view. The prism has six flat faces in all.

pages.text: An edge is where two faces meet. A rectangular prism has twelve edges. How many can you see? A vertex is where a base and two faces meet. The word vertices is plural for vertex. A rectangular prism has eight vertices. How many can you see?
pages.brief: A rectangular prism is shown with its straight edges and sharp vertices visible. Two faces meet along an edge, and a base and two faces meet at a vertex. The prism has twelve edges and eight vertices in all.

pages.text: Hardware Store Issac looks for rectangular prisms in the hardware store. He knows they have: • six faces • two bases that are opposite each other • twelve edges • eight vertices.
pages.brief: Issac stands in a hardware store, looking around at objects shaped like rectangular prisms. Hardware-store goods and shelves surround him as he studies their six faces, two opposite bases, twelve edges, and eight vertices, searching for rectangular prisms among the items.

pages.text: How many rectangular prisms do you see?
pages.brief: A collection of rectangular prisms is arranged in a hardware-store setting for counting. Several box-shaped solids of different sizes sit among hardware items, with flat faces, straight edges, and corners visible, inviting the viewer to look carefully and count the rectangular prisms.

pages.text: Cubes A cube is another type of solid that is also a rectangular prism. It has six faces, eight vertices, and twelve edges.
pages.brief: A cube sits alone, with six square faces, eight vertices, and twelve edges visible from different angles. The solid is a type of rectangular prism, and its straight edges and corners are clearly shown so its shape can be examined.

pages.text: Look at the orange face on the cube. It is a square. The blue and yellow faces are also squares. All six faces are squares with equal edges all around.
pages.brief: A cube is shown with an orange face facing forward, a blue face beside it, and a yellow face above. Each visible face is a square, and all six faces have equal edges all around. The cube's straight edges meet at clear corners.

pages.text: Toy Store Tanya looks for cubes in the toy store. She knows they have: • six square faces • eight vertices • twelve equal edges.
pages.brief: Tanya stands in a toy store, looking at toys shaped like cubes. Cube-shaped blocks and playthings are arranged around her, and she studies their six square faces, eight vertices, and twelve equal edges as she searches for cubes among the toys.

pages.text: How many cubes can you see?
pages.brief: A group of cubes is arranged in a toy-store display for counting. Several cube-shaped toys and blocks of different colors sit together, with square faces and equal edges visible, inviting the viewer to count how many cubes are shown.

pages.text: Spheres This solid is a sphere. It has no flat faces, edges, or vertices.
pages.brief: A single sphere rests alone against a plain background. Its surface is completely curved and smooth, with no flat faces, no straight edges, and no vertices anywhere on it. It looks round from every side.

pages.text: A sphere has a curved surface and nothing else. All points on a sphere’s curved surface are the same distance from the center.
pages.brief: A sphere is shown as a round solid whose entire outside is a curved surface. All points on that surface lie the same distance from the center, so the shape looks perfectly even and round in every direction.

pages.text: Sports Shop Leara looks for spheres in the sports shop. She knows they have: • no faces, edges, or vertices • surfaces on which all points are the same distance from the center.
pages.brief: Leara stands in a sports shop, looking around at balls and other sports items shaped like spheres. She studies their curved surfaces, knowing spheres have no faces, edges, or vertices and every point on the surface is the same distance from the center.

pages.text: How many spheres can you see?
pages.brief: A collection of spheres is arranged in a sports-shop setting for counting. Several round balls of different sizes and colors sit together, each with a curved surface and no edges or vertices, inviting the viewer to count how many spheres are shown.

pages.text: Cylinders This solid is a cylinder. It has two faces. The faces are circles. No matter how hard you look, you will not find a single vertex on a cylinder. Cylinders also have curved surfaces.
pages.brief: A cylinder is shown standing upright. It has two flat circular faces, one at the top and one at the bottom, and a curved surface between them. No vertex can be found anywhere on the cylinder.

pages.text: Cones This solid is a cone. A cone has only one face that is a circle.
pages.brief: A cone stands alone with one flat circular face at its base and a curved surface rising to a point on top. It has only one face shaped like a circle, and its curved side narrows upward.

pages.text: House and Neighborhood Ruben and Megan look for cylinders and cones around their house and neighborhood. They know cylinders have: • two faces shaped like a circle • no vertices • curved surfaces They know cones have: • one face shaped like a circle.
pages.brief: Ruben and Megan walk around their house and neighborhood, looking for cylinders and cones. They notice cylinder shapes with two circular faces and no vertices, and cone shapes with one circular face, among the buildings and objects nearby.

pages.text: How many cylinders and cones do you see?
pages.brief: A neighborhood scene shows a group of cylinders and cones for counting. Several cylindrical and cone-shaped objects appear around houses and nearby surroundings, with circular faces and curved surfaces visible, inviting the viewer to count how many of each shape can be seen.

pages.text: Square Pyramids This solid is a square pyramid. It has four faces that are shaped like triangles. They are connected by four edges. It also has a face that is shaped like a square. There is one vertex on top of a square pyramid.
pages.brief: A square pyramid stands alone. Four triangular faces rise from a square base, connected by four edges, and a single vertex sits at the very top of the pyramid. The base is a flat square face.

pages.text: When a square pyramid is turned over, you can see four more vertices on the bottom. There are five vertices in all, including the one on top. It is a square pyramid because the face on the base is square. There are four more edges that connect the triangular faces to the base. Square pyramids have eight edges in all.
pages.brief: A square pyramid is turned over, showing four vertices on the bottom and one on top. The square base is visible, and four edges connect the triangular faces to the base; altogether the pyramid has five vertices and eight edges.

pages.text: Around the World Here’s an amazing group of square pyramids! You would have to go to Giza, in Egypt, to find them.
pages.brief: A group of square pyramids stands at Giza in Egypt. The enormous stone pyramids rise from the desert, with triangular faces and square bases, showing an amazing real-world example of square pyramids in a famous place.

pages.text: Solids really are all around. Ruben and his friends saw them in their neighborhood and across the world. Where can you find solids around you?
pages.brief: Ruben and his friends stand together, looking around their neighborhood and thinking about solids across the world. Solid figures appear in the shapes of nearby objects and in famous structures, and the children wonder where else solids can be found.

pages.text: Draw lines to match each shape to its name. rectangular prism cylinder cone square pyramid sphere cube.
pages.brief: Six solid figures are spaced out for a matching activity: a rectangular prism, a cylinder, a cone, a square pyramid, a sphere, and a cube. Blank spaces beside each solid are ready for lines to be drawn connecting each shape to its matching partner.

books.title: What's Your Money Worth?
books.art_why: Real money, markets, workers, children and toys are everyday subjects that can be photographed today.

pages.text: What’s Your Money Worth?
pages.brief: A dollar bill and a dollar coin rest side by side in a clear, simple view. The two kinds of money are arranged for comparison, inviting a look at how much each piece is worth and what money value means.

pages.text: Making One Dollar with a Dollar Bill and a Dollar Coin Megan has a dollar coin. Tony has a dollar bill. A dollar coin and a dollar bill are both worth one dollar.
pages.brief: Megan holds a dollar coin and Tony holds a dollar bill, standing together and comparing the two kinds of money. They look at the coin and the bill, both worth one dollar, in a plain, clear view.

pages.text: Making One Dollar with Fifty-Cent Coins Tony has two fifty-cent coins. Megan has a dollar bill. Two fifty-cent coins and a dollar bill are both worth one dollar. Making One Dollar with Quarters Megan has four quarters. Tony has a dollar bill. Four quarters and a dollar bill are both worth one dollar. What’s Your Money Worth?
pages.brief: Tony holds two fifty-cent coins beside Megan and her dollar bill. Then Megan holds four quarters beside Tony and his dollar bill. The pairs of money are placed for comparison, each set making one dollar in a clear view.

pages.text: Making One Dollar with Nickels Megan has a dollar bill. Tony has twenty nickels. Tony groups his nickels in pairs. He skip-counts to see how much money he has. By what number does he skip-count? A dollar bill and twenty nickels are both worth one dollar.
pages.brief: Megan holds a dollar bill while Tony places twenty nickels in pairs. Tony groups the nickels two by two and skip-counts them, checking how much money he has beside Megan's dollar bill. The paired nickels and the dollar bill are shown together for comparison.

pages.text: Making One Dollar with Pennies Kaya has a dollar bill. Ruben has one hundred pennies. He groups them into ten stacks. Each stack has ten pennies. One hundred pennies and a dollar bill are both worth one dollar. What’s Your Money Worth?
pages.brief: Kaya holds a dollar bill while Ruben arranges one hundred pennies into ten stacks. Each stack holds ten pennies. Ruben and Kaya look at the stacks and the dollar bill together, comparing the pennies with the one-dollar bill.

pages.text: Bills Greater Than One Dollar Rose works in the market. A shopper buys twenty-six dollars’ worth of food. He pays with five five-dollar bills and a one-dollar bill. Here’s how Rose groups the money to count it.
pages.brief: Rose works in the market. A shopper buys twenty-six dollars' worth of food and pays with five five-dollar bills and a one-dollar bill. Rose groups the bills in front of her to count the money.

pages.text: Counting Bills and Coins The next shopper pays with bills and coins. Her total is three dollars and sixteen cents or $3.16. Rose first groups the bills and coins. She orders the coins from greatest value to least value. What’s Your Money Worth?
pages.brief: The next shopper pays Rose with bills and coins. The total is three dollars and sixteen cents. Rose first groups the bills and coins, then orders the coins from greatest value to least value as she prepares to count them.

pages.text: Money and Things Have Value Things such as food and clothing have a value. This means they are worth something. Money has value, too. It can be used to buy food and clothing. When people buy things, they are giving money for something of equal value. Work has value also. People are paid money for their work, or jobs. The owner of the market pays Rose money for doing her job.
pages.brief: Food and clothing are shown with money, because things and money have value. People use money to buy food and clothing. Work has value too: the owner of the market pays Rose money for doing her job.

pages.text: Ruben earns two dollars and seventy-five cents a week when he feeds Mrs. Lee’s dog. Mrs. Lee has these bills and coins shown below. one-dollar bills five-dollar bill dimes nickels pennies quarters How could Mrs. Lee count out the exact money to pay Ruben for one week’s work with the fewest coins?
pages.brief: Ruben feeds Mrs. Lee's dog, work that earns him two dollars and seventy-five cents a week. Mrs. Lee has one-dollar bills, a five-dollar bill, dimes, nickels, pennies, and quarters. She considers how to count out the exact money for Ruben's week of work with the fewest coins.

pages.text: Making Exact Amounts Ruben has earned eight dollars and twenty-five cents for a few weeks of work. He wants to buy a toy robot. Will he have enough money? $7.85 What’s Your Money Worth?
pages.brief: Ruben has earned eight dollars and twenty-five cents from a few weeks of work. He looks at a toy robot that costs seven dollars and eighty-five cents, wondering whether he has enough money to buy it.

pages.text: Ruben has the money shown below. He counts out the exact amount he will need. What does exact amount mean? How can Ruben count out the exact amount?
pages.brief: Ruben has bills and coins shown before him. He counts out the exact amount he will need, checking what exact amount means and how to count it carefully from the money he has. The money is laid out for counting.

pages.text: Kesha wants to buy a pin for her mother. She has these dollar bills and coins. What is the value of the pin? Does Kesha have the exact amount that she needs to buy it? What’s Your Money Worth?
pages.brief: Kesha holds dollar bills and coins, wanting to buy a pin for her mother. The pin is shown with her money. Kesha thinks about the value of the pin and whether she has the exact amount needed to buy it.

pages.text: Kesha uses this money to buy the pin. Is the money equal to, more than, or less than the value of the pin?
pages.brief: Kesha uses her money to buy the pin. She gives the bills and coins for the pin and checks whether the money is equal to, more than, or less than the pin's value. The pin and the money are shown together.

pages.text: Making Change Tanner also wants to buy a pin for his mother. He has these dollar bills. $2.84 What is the value, or price, of the pin? Does Tanner have the exact amount he needs to buy it? What’s Your Money Worth?
pages.brief: Tanner holds dollar bills, wanting to buy a pin for his mother. The pin is shown with the amount two dollars and eighty-four cents. Tanner asks what the pin's value is and whether he has the exact amount he needs.

pages.text: Tanner has more than the exact amount of money to buy the pin. He can buy it and get back money called change. How much change did Tanner get back?
pages.brief: Tanner has more than the exact amount of money for the pin, so he buys it and gets money back as change. He receives the change and sees how much he got back after paying for the pin.

pages.text: Ruben has a dollar bill. He uses it to buy a ball. How much change will Ruben get back? Count on from the cost of the ball until you get to one dollar. What’s Your Money Worth?
pages.brief: Ruben holds a dollar bill and uses it to buy a ball. He counts on from the cost of the ball until he reaches one dollar, working out how much change he will get back after buying the ball.

pages.text: Isaac buys a wind-up toy. $2.52 He wants as few coins as possible for his change. He uses this money for the toy.
pages.brief: Isaac buys a wind-up toy that costs two dollars and fifty-two cents. He wants as few coins as possible for his change. Isaac uses this money for the toy, with the toy and the money shown together.

pages.text: Does Isaac have the exact amount? By spending three dollars and two cents, he gets back two quarters. He has more than the exact amount and gets back just a couple of coins. $2.52 What’s Your Money Worth?
pages.brief: Does Isaac have the exact amount? By spending three dollars and two cents for the two-dollar-and-fifty-two-cent toy, he gets back two quarters. He has more than the exact amount and gets back just a couple of coins.

pages.text: Phoebe has these bills and coins to buy some hair clips. Phoebe gets the hair clips and this change. What coins or bills did Phoebe use to pay for the hair clips?
pages.brief: Phoebe has bills and coins to buy some hair clips. She gets the hair clips and some change. Phoebe's money, the hair clips, and the change are shown together, inviting a look at which coins or bills she used to pay.

pages.text: Trading Money of Equal Value Megan has a five-dollar bill. She needs two quarters for the vending machine. She asks Tony to exchange money with her. Can Tony exchange some of his money for Megan’s five-dollar bill and also have two quarters left for the machine? What’s Your Money Worth?
pages.brief: Megan holds a five-dollar bill and needs two quarters for the vending machine. She asks Tony to exchange money with her. Tony has his own money with him, and they consider whether he can exchange money for her five-dollar bill and still have two quarters left.

pages.text: Megan gives Tony her five-dollar bill. The money that Tony gives back to Megan is equal to her five-dollar bill. Does Tony still have two quarters left to use in the machine?
pages.brief: Megan gives Tony her five-dollar bill. Tony gives Megan money equal to her five-dollar bill. After the exchange, Tony checks whether he still has two quarters left to use in the vending machine. The exchange is shown with the bill and coins.

pages.text: If you had three dollars, which item would you buy? Which bills or coins would you get back for change? Think about what you learned about what your money is worth. Toy Cars What’s Your Money Worth?
pages.brief: Toy cars are displayed for choice, with three dollars in bills or coins nearby. A buyer with three dollars would choose an item and think about which bills or coins would come back as change, using what was learned about money value.

books.title: Tornadoes
books.art_why: Tornadoes are real weather events that can be photographed.

pages.text: Introduction What can lift roofs from buildings and sweep houses into the air? Tornadoes can. Tornadoes come in many sizes. Some tornadoes are only a few feet (1 m) across. Others are more than a mile (2 km) wide. Some tornadoes touch down for a short time. Others travel for hundreds of miles.
pages.brief: A huge tornado rips the roof off a building and sweeps a house into the air, while smaller tornadoes touch down nearby. Some funnels are only a few feet across; others stretch more than a mile wide. One tornado briefly touches the ground, and another travels far across the land.

pages.text: How Tornadoes Form Why do tornadoes happen? Scientists are not sure. Tornadoes come from giant thunderstorms called supercells. A supercell happens when warm, moist air rises to mix with cold, dry air.
pages.brief: A giant supercell thunderstorm towers over open land. Warm, moist air rises from the ground while cold, dry air sinks toward it. The two air masses meet inside the huge storm cloud, creating swirling motion.

pages.text: The mixing of cold and warm air causes the air to spin. The spinning wind turns into a cloud in a funnel shape. As the cloud turns, the wind becomes stronger. When the funnel cloud touches the ground, it is a tornado.
pages.brief: Inside the storm, cold and warm air mix and set the wind spinning. The spinning wind lowers from the cloud in a funnel shape. As the funnel turns, the wind grows stronger. The funnel cloud reaches down and touches the ground, becoming a tornado.

pages.text: How a Tornado Forms sp supercell thundercloud warm air rises air keeps spinning inside the thundercloud rain and hail begin to fall funnel cloud the funnel cloud touches down and travels over land the tornado damages anything in its path flying debris.
pages.brief: A view shows a supercell thundercloud with warm air rising and spinning inside. Rain and hail fall from the dark cloud. A funnel cloud reaches down and touches the land, then travels forward. The tornado tears across the ground, damaging everything in its path and throwing debris into the air.

pages.text: Where Tornadoes Form Tornadoes may be hard to measure, but scientists have a good idea where they’ll strike. It’s true that a tornado can hit anywhere in the world at any time. Most tornadoes happen in the central part of the United States. This area is called Tornado Alley. Tornado Alley Canada COLD, DRY AIR COLD, DRY AIR Nebraska Nebraska United States Colorado Colorado Kansas Kansas TORNADO ALLEY TORNADO ALLEY Oklahoma Oklahoma Texas Texas WARM, MOIST AIR WARM, MOIST AIR Mexico.
pages.brief: A map view of the central United States shows the Tornado Alley region stretching across Texas, Oklahoma, Kansas, Nebraska, and Colorado. Cold, dry air moves down from Canada, while warm, moist air flows up from Mexico. These air masses meet over the central plains.

pages.text: The giant tornado that hit Moore, Oklahoma, in 2013 left behind a clear path. More than one thousand tornadoes strike Tornado Alley each year.
pages.brief: A giant tornado has cut a clear, dark path through Moore, Oklahoma, leaving damaged ground and debris behind. The scar of the storm stretches across the landscape. More than a thousand tornadoes strike Tornado Alley each year, and this one left a visible trail.

pages.text: Tornado Safety There is no way to be sure that a tornado will strike. The National Weather Service (NWS) tries to help people stay safe during tornadoes. If they put out a tornado watch, a tornado might strike. If they put out a tornado warning, a tornado has been spotted.
pages.brief: People at the National Weather Service monitor storms and share safety information. A tornado watch means a tornado might strike; a tornado warning means one has been spotted. The weather service works to help people stay safe when dangerous storms threaten.

pages.text: If there is a tornado warning, it’s important to get to a safe place. Go indoors. The safest place is a basement. If you can’t get to a basement, go into a closet or bathroom. Stay away from windows.
pages.brief: When a tornado warning sounds, a person hurries indoors to a safe place. They go down into a basement, or into a small closet or bathroom if no basement is available. They stay far away from windows as the storm threatens outside.

pages.text: The spinning air in a tornado makes things fly around. This can be dangerous. It’s always important to protect your head. You should get close to the ground. Go under a desk or table. You can even lie down in a bathtub.
pages.brief: Spinning tornado air sends objects flying around, making the situation dangerous. A person crouches close to the ground and protects their head. They take shelter under a sturdy desk or table, or lie down inside a bathtub to stay safer from flying debris.

pages.text: If you are in a tall building, go to the stairs. If you are in a car, safely find lower ground and lie down. Otherwise, wear your seatbelt and lean forward. If you are outside, lie down on the ground. It isn’t safe to stay inside a mobile home in a tornado. It is better to go into a car or outside. A tornado that hit Kansas in 2003 was so powerful that it caused a child’s bicycle to wrap around a tree. Famous Tornadoes.
pages.brief: In a tall building, a person goes to the stairs. In a car, someone finds lower ground and lies down, or wears a seatbelt and leans forward. Outside, a person lies on the ground. A powerful Kansas tornado in 2003 wrapped a child’s bicycle around a tree.

pages.text: Conclusion Tornadoes are scary examples of the power of nature. People still have many questions about tornadoes. What causes a tornado? What is it really like inside a tornado? Maybe we will find out one day.
pages.brief: A tornado looms as a scary example of nature’s power. People still have many questions about these storms. They wonder what causes a tornado and what it is really like inside one. Maybe one day we will find out.

books.title: Tokyo Imperial Palace
books.art_why: The book includes the early 1600s castle and the 1657 tower fire, before photographs, so drawings suit the historical scenes.

pages.text: Tokyo Imperial Palace.
pages.brief: The Tokyo Imperial Palace is shown in Tokyo as the book's subject. The palace building and its grounds are presented clearly, with the city setting around it. The scene focuses on the place itself, with no people or extra events.

pages.text: Tokyo Tokyo Imperial Imperial Palace Palace.
pages.brief: The Tokyo Imperial Palace appears again as the focus, located in Tokyo. The view presents the palace and its setting as a calm, important place. No people or additional actions are shown; the image keeps attention on the palace itself.

pages.text: A Peaceful Place The city of Tokyo is very busy and modern. The Imperial Palace sits in the middle of that city. It is a peaceful place. The emperor and empress of Japan live there.
pages.brief: The busy, modern city of Tokyo fills the background, while the Imperial Palace sits in the middle of it as a peaceful place. The emperor and empress of Japan are shown living there, within the calm palace grounds.

pages.text: Where Is It? Tokyo is on the east coast of Japan. The Imperial Palace lies in the heart of Tokyo. It is near the Japanese National Theatre and Tokyo Disneyland.
pages.brief: Tokyo is shown on the east coast of Japan. The Imperial Palace lies in the heart of Tokyo, near the Japanese National Theatre and Tokyo Disneyland. The view places the palace within the city and shows its nearby landmarks.

pages.text: History of the Palace A castle has stood on the site of the Imperial Palace for hundreds of years. In the early 1600s, a powerful lord built a grand castle called Edo Castle there. Sadly, its beautiful main tower burned down in 1657. Visitors can still see the stone base of that tower on the grounds of the Imperial Palace.
pages.brief: In the early 1600s, a powerful lord builds a grand castle called Edo Castle on the site of today's Imperial Palace. The castle's beautiful main tower burns down in 1657. Visitors today can still see the tower's stone base on the palace grounds.

pages.text: In the 1800s, the emperor decided to move his home to the site of Edo Castle. He ordered workers to build a new palace there. They finished building the new Imperial Palace in 1888. The new palace looked Japanese on the outside. Inside, though, there were many European decorations and furniture.
pages.brief: In the 1800s, the emperor decides to move his home to the site of Edo Castle. Workers build a new palace there and finish in 1888. The palace looks Japanese on the outside, while inside it has many European decorations and furniture.

pages.text: During World War II, the United States bombed the area around the palace. The palace was made of wood, so it was damaged by fires. After the war, Japan built the palace again. This time, workers used cement instead of wood. They finished in 1968. The building we can see today looks very much like it did before the war.
pages.brief: During World War II, the United States bombs the area around the palace. Fires damage the wooden palace. After the war, Japan rebuilds the palace using cement instead of wood, finishing in 1968. The building seen today looks much like it did before the war.

pages.text: Building the Walls The palace grounds have stone walls around them. Workers used a special way of building to make them. The builders stacked stones to form the walls. They did not use any mortar to keep the stones together. That way, all the rainwater could drain out through the cracks. Even heavy rain would not damage the walls. This way of building also helped protect the walls in an earthquake. Some of the stone walls from the early 1600s still stand today. Traditionally, Japanese buildings were made of wood, like this tea house on the palace grounds.
pages.brief: Stone walls surround the palace grounds. Builders stack stones without mortar so rainwater drains through the cracks and heavy rain does not damage the walls. The same method helps protect the walls in an earthquake. Some stone walls from the early 1600s still stand, and a wooden tea house is shown on the grounds.

pages.text: The Tokyo Imperial Palace Science Museum Tokyo National Museum of Modern Art Kitanomaru Park Museum of Imperial Collections East Gardens Imperial Palace Outer Garden Imperial Palace Nijubashi Bridge The Imperial Palace grounds • are about 115 hectares (284 acres) in area • are surrounded by moats • have defensive stone walls, some from the Edo period • are home to several museums.
pages.brief: The Imperial Palace grounds cover about 115 hectares (284 acres), surrounded by moats and defensive stone walls, some from the Edo period. The grounds are home to several museums, including the Tokyo Imperial Palace Science Museum, Tokyo National Museum of Modern Art, and Museum of Imperial Collections. Kitanomaru Park, East Gardens, Imperial Palace Outer Garden, and Nijubashi Bridge are nearby.

pages.text: Four Sections The Imperial Palace in Tokyo has four areas. They are the Imperial Palace Outer Garden, Kitanomaru Park, the East Gardens, and the Imperial Palace inner grounds.
pages.brief: The Imperial Palace in Tokyo is shown divided into four areas: the Imperial Palace Outer Garden, Kitanomaru Park, the East Gardens, and the Imperial Palace inner grounds. The view presents each section as part of the whole palace site.

pages.text: The Imperial Palace Outer Garden is a free park. The Nijubashi Bridge is a famous bridge in this area. The East Gardens are also open for people to visit. The East Gardens are beautiful all year. Some of the oldest buildings and walls in this area are from the 1600s.
pages.brief: The Imperial Palace Outer Garden is shown as a free park with the famous Nijubashi Bridge. Nearby, the East Gardens are open for visitors and look beautiful all year. Some of the oldest buildings and walls in this area date from the 1600s.

pages.text: The emperor and empress live on the Imperial Palace grounds. The palace itself is also in this area of the site. The palace is a large building. It has two stories aboveground and one story below the ground. The emperor does his work for the government there. He takes part in special events. He throws big parties for important visitors.
pages.brief: The emperor and empress live on the Imperial Palace grounds. The large palace building has two stories aboveground and one below. Inside, the emperor does government work, takes part in special events, and throws big parties for important visitors.

pages.text: Natural Beauty The emperor protects nature at the Imperial Palace. More than 3,600 species of animals and insects live there. So do more than 1,300 species of plants. It is amazing to find so much natural beauty in such a big city.
pages.brief: The emperor protects nature at the Imperial Palace. More than 3,600 species of animals and insects live there, and more than 1,300 species of plants grow there too. The scene shows surprising natural beauty inside a very big city.

pages.text: An Important Landmark The Imperial Palace is important even today. Therefore, the government takes very good care of it. Many people exercise on the palace grounds. Many others visit the palace for fun. Every spring, one million visitors come to see the cherry trees bloom there. People enjoy the beauty and history of the Imperial Palace.
pages.brief: The Imperial Palace is an important landmark, so the government takes very good care of it. Many people exercise on the palace grounds, and many others visit for fun. Every spring, one million visitors come to see the cherry trees bloom, enjoying the beauty and history of the palace.

books.title: Animal Defenses
books.art_why: real animals and natural defenses are shown

pages.text: Introduction In the wild, many animals eat other animals. These predators are always on the hunt for their next meal. Their prey, however, don’t just sit around waiting to be eaten. These animals have developed many ways to defend themselves.
pages.brief: In a wild setting, predators hunt other animals for their next meal, while prey animals do not wait to be eaten. The scene shows prey animals using several different ways to defend themselves against predators.

pages.text: Claws, Teeth, Spikes Lions, tigers, and bears have sharp teeth and claws. Some smaller animals, like house cats and raccoons, also have them.
pages.brief: A lion, a tiger, and a bear are shown with sharp teeth and claws. Nearby, a house cat and a raccoon also show their sharp teeth and claws in a natural setting where these animals live.

pages.text: Some animals have sharp spikes to keep predators away. Porcupines are covered in sharp spikes called quills. The quills are made of the same stuff as human hair and fingernails. The quills can stick in predators’ skin like needles. Hedgehogs also have quills. When hedgehogs are attacked, they roll up in a ball so all their quills point out.
pages.brief: A porcupine is covered in sharp quills made of the same material as human hair and fingernails. The quills can stick into a predator’s skin like needles. A hedgehog rolls into a ball so all its quills point outward toward an attacker.

pages.text: Animals That Use Venom Some animals can hurt or even kill predators with a bite or a sting. These animals deliver venom to defend themselves.
pages.brief: Some animals are shown defending themselves by delivering venom through a bite or a sting. The scene focuses on animals that can hurt or even kill predators with venom, using it as a way to stay safe.

pages.text: Some snakes have venom. The venom in the bite of a king cobra is strong enough to kill an elephant! Bees, wasps, and some ants also have venom. All spiders have fangs, and most spiders have venom, too.
pages.brief: A king cobra is shown with venom strong enough to kill an elephant. Bees, wasps, and some ants also have venom. A spider displays fangs, and most spiders have venom, too, in a natural setting.

pages.text: Animals That Use Poison Some animals are poisonous. That means their bodies release a dangerous substance when another animal attacks or tries to eat them. The puffer fish has poison in its skin, and some puffer fish also have spikes to keep enemies away. The poison tastes bad to other fish, and it can be deadly.
pages.brief: A puffer fish is shown with poison in its skin and spikes that keep enemies away. The poison tastes bad to other fish and can be deadly. The scene shows a poisonous animal releasing a dangerous substance when another animal attacks or tries to eat it.

pages.text: The golden poison frog is one of the most poisonous animals in the world. It is only about 5 centimeters (2 in.) long, but its skin is coated with a strong poison. Venom or Poison? Venom and poison are not the same thing. Poison soaks into the skin, is eaten, or is breathed in. Venom is delivered through a bite or sting. A scorpion uses venom to defend itself, while a cuttlefish uses poison.
pages.brief: A tiny golden poison frog, about five centimeters long, is shown with skin coated in strong poison. A scorpion is shown using venom to defend itself, while a cuttlefish is shown using poison. The scene contrasts venom delivered through a bite or sting with poison that soaks in, is eaten, or is breathed in.

pages.text: Camouflage Some animals defend themselves by using camouflage, or blending in with the world around them. Some squid can change their skin color to hide in the water or to confuse predators. Some insects are the same color as the leaves or branches they live on. For example, the dead-leaf butterfly really looks like a dead leaf when its wings are closed.
pages.brief: A squid is shown changing its skin color to hide in the water or confuse predators. Some insects are the same color as the leaves or branches where they live. A dead-leaf butterfly looks like a dead leaf when its wings are closed.

pages.text: Zebras are black with white stripes and travel in groups. Their predators have trouble seeing where one zebra ends and another one begins. This makes it more difficult for predators such as lions to hunt zebras.
pages.brief: Zebras with black and white stripes are shown traveling in a group. Their predators have trouble seeing where one zebra ends and another begins. This makes it more difficult for predators such as lions to hunt the zebras.

pages.text: Other Defenses Most predators catch live prey, so some animals defend themselves by playing dead. The opossum is famous for playing dead when it is afraid. If a hognose snake is attacked, it puffs up and hisses just like a cobra. If that fails, it rolls onto its back and releases a stinky liquid. When it does, it looks and smells dead.
pages.brief: An opossum is shown playing dead because it is afraid. A hognose snake puffs up and hisses like a cobra; if that fails, it rolls onto its back and releases a stinky liquid. Then it looks and smells dead.

pages.text: Some animals, like deer, defend themselves by being faster than the predators that hunt them. Other animals defend themselves by leaving body parts behind. Many lizards lose their tails when attacked. This distracts predators and makes it easier for the lizards to run quickly. Some lizards can even grow their tails back later!
pages.brief: A deer is shown defending itself by being faster than the predators that hunt it. Many lizards lose their tails when attacked, which distracts predators and helps the lizards run quickly. Some lizards can even grow their tails back later.

pages.text: Conclusion Predators and prey are both necessary in the wild. Both add to the balance of the natural world. Different types of defenses give all animals a fighting chance.
pages.brief: Predators and prey are shown together in the wild, both adding to the balance of the natural world. Different types of defenses give all animals a fighting chance to survive against the predators that hunt them.

books.title: The Baobab
books.art_why: The book includes long-ago tree dwellers and a legend, so drawn scenes suit the whole book.

pages.text: Where in the World Do Baobabs Grow? ASIA The Lands of Africa Africa has large, sandy deserts. It has thick, dark jungles. It also has open, grassy plains. The plains, known as the African savanna, are not just made up of grass, however. Strange, ancient trees grow there, too. They are called baobabs. These “trees of life” have helped the people and other animals of the savanna for thousands of years.
pages.brief: A broad African landscape shows large sandy deserts, thick dark jungles and open grassy savanna plains. Strange ancient baobab trees rise from the grassy plains. People and wildlife live nearby, showing how these trees have helped life on the savanna for thousands of years.

pages.text: Giants of the Savanna Finding a baobab is easy. These trees rise high above the flat plains. A full-grown baobab can be 18 meters (59 ft.) tall. That’s taller than a five-story building!
pages.brief: A full-grown baobab rises high above the flat savanna plains. The tree is as tall as a five-story building, with a wide trunk and spreading branches. Smaller plants and open grassland stretch around it under a bright sky.

pages.text: Baobab trees have thick, barrel- shaped trunks. The oldest trees have trunks that are 9 meters (30 ft.) across. Like barrels, the trunks hold a lot of water. This is important because the savanna is a dry place. Being able to store water helps baobabs survive in the savanna. Baobabs also have strange branches. Their branches spread out like roots. When a baobab sheds its leaves, the tree looks as if it is upside down!
pages.brief: A close view of a baobab shows its thick, barrel-shaped trunk and branches spreading like roots. The oldest trunks are very wide and hold water inside. With its leaves gone, the tree looks as if it is upside down on the dry savanna.

pages.text: The Baobab’s Gifts The wildlife and people of the savanna get many things from the baobab. The tree’s soft wood is filled with water. The leafy branches give cool shade from the hot Sun.
pages.brief: A leafy baobab casts cool shade over people and savanna wildlife on a hot, sunny plain. Its soft wood is shown holding water. The tree stands as a source of many gifts for the people and animals living around it.

pages.text: Bats drink sweet nectar from the tree’s white flowers. The flowers grow into fruit. The fruit bakes in the sun and dries. Its green coating turns into a hard shell. Then it is picked by hand.
pages.brief: At dusk, bats drink sweet nectar from white baobab flowers. The flowers grow into fruit, which bakes and dries in the hot sun until its green coating becomes a hard shell. A hand reaches up to pick the ripe fruit from the tree.

pages.text: Baobab fruit is packed with vitamins. It has more vitamin C than an orange and as much calcium as milk! People use the fruit to make a healthy, tasty drink. It can also be used to make a kind of ice cream. Do You Know? Some people use baobab fruit and bark as medicine. A tea made from its bark is thought to cure stomachaches. The leaves may lower a fever. Oil from baobab seeds might help ease a toothache. Baobab fruit is also thought to help sore bones.
pages.brief: A baobab fruit is shown with an orange and a glass of milk to compare its vitamins and calcium. People make a healthy drink and a kind of ice cream from the fruit. Bark, leaves and seeds are gathered for tea, fever relief, toothache oil and sore bones.

pages.text: A Different Kind of Tree House Baobab trees are useful in other ways, too. People weave long strings from the tree’s bark to make cloth, rope, and baskets. They use the roots to make red dye.
pages.brief: People weave long strings from baobab bark into cloth, rope and baskets. Others use the tree’s roots to make red dye. The scene shows people working with bark fibres and root dye on the savanna, turning parts of the baobab into everyday useful objects.

pages.text: The trees also give shelter to animals. Insects, lizards, monkeys, and other animals live in their branches and trunks. Long ago, people, too, used these trees as shelter. They did not make tree houses in their branches. They did not cut the wood to build houses. Instead, they lived inside a tree’s hollow trunk!
pages.brief: Insects, lizards and monkeys live among a baobab’s branches and trunk. Inside a hollow trunk, long-ago people make a simple shelter, resting within the tree. They have not built a tree house in the branches or cut wood for a house.

pages.text: Baobab trunks have been used as homes and barns. People have found all sorts of uses for these trees!
pages.brief: A hollow baobab trunk is shown as a home and as a barn. People live inside one tree, while another trunk holds stored goods. Around them, different parts of the baobab are used in everyday life, showing the many practical uses people have found for these trees.

pages.text: Hollow Trees A baobab is hollow because it does not have a single trunk. Instead, it has several stems. The stems grow and attach to each other, forming a ring. Bark covers the stems and makes them look like one trunk.
pages.brief: A cutaway view of a baobab trunk shows several stems growing together and attaching to form a ring. Bark covers the stems so they look like one trunk. The open centre makes the tree hollow, even though it stands as a single giant on the savanna.

pages.text: Dying Giants Giant baobab trees have stood guard in Africa for centuries. Sadly, some of the oldest ones are dying off. At least nine trees that were thousands of years old have died since 2005. No one is sure why the trees are dying. Some people think the trees might have become sick over time. Other people worry that it is because Earth is getting warmer. Still others think it is just because the trees were old. Legend of the Baobab There are many stories about baobabs. One explains why the trees look so strange. According to the legend, the African god Thora had a baobab tree in his garden. He did not like how it looked, so he pulled it up and threw it over the garden wall. The poor baobab fell to Earth and landed upside down!
pages.brief: Some of Africa’s oldest giant baobabs stand weathered and dying on the savanna; nine ancient trees have died since 2005. Nearby, a legendary scene shows the African god Thora pulling a baobab from his garden and throwing it over the wall, so it lands upside down on Earth.

pages.text: Without baobabs, life in Africa would not be the same. These giants of the savanna have so much to offer. Hopefully, people can look forward to their plentiful gifts for years to come.
pages.brief: A wide African savanna scene shows baobabs standing among people and wildlife, with their fruit, shade and shelter valued. The trees are presented as giants with much to offer, and the scene looks ahead to their gifts continuing for years to come.

books.title: Spiders
books.art_why: Real spiders, webs, and habitats exist today and can be photographed.

pages.text: Spiders.
pages.brief: Several spiders of different sizes and kinds are shown together in a natural outdoor setting, giving a close-up view of their bodies and legs. The spiders rest among natural surfaces, and the image introduces the variety of spiders.

pages.text: Introduction Do you jump when a spider crosses your path? Spiders may make some people nervous, yet they are mostly harmless to humans. More than forty thousand kinds of spiders live all over the world. They range in size from the head of a pin to a large dinner plate. The smallest may be lighter than a feather, while the heaviest can weigh as much as a softball.
pages.brief: A spider crosses a woodland path while a person's feet stand nearby, suggesting someone noticing it. Around them, small and large spiders are shown at different scales, from pinhead-sized to dinner-plate-sized, with feather-light and softball-heavy examples shown by size comparison.

pages.text: Traits Although spiders look like insects, they are different in many ways. Spiders have eight legs. Insects have only six. Spiders have two body parts including the head. Insects have three body parts including the head. Most spiders have eight eyes, and most insects have only two. Spiders do not have wings. Most insects do.
pages.brief: A spider and an insect are shown close together in a natural setting. The spider clearly has eight legs, two body parts, eight eyes, and no wings, while the insect beside it has six legs, three body parts, two eyes, and wings.

pages.text: Life Cycle A female spider can lay thousands of eggs. After they hatch, the babies often stay near the mother until they can live on their own. Many spiders only live for a couple of years. Some, such as female tarantulas, can live up to thirty years.
pages.brief: A female spider rests near a large cluster of eggs and many tiny spiderlings gathered around her. Nearby, a female tarantula is shown as an example of a spider that can live for many years.

pages.text: Diet Spiders eat about half a billion tons of insects each year. Without spiders, insects would destroy much of our food crops. Spiders also keep the number of pests such as mosquitos under control. Most spiders use their fangs to bite prey and inject venom—a poisonous liquid. Fangs work like a needle.
pages.brief: A spider holds an insect prey and uses its fangs to bite it, showing venom being injected like a needle. Nearby, mosquitoes and other pest insects swarm near green food crops, illustrating the many insects that spiders help keep under control.

pages.text: Webs and Silk Some spiders make webs, which come in many beautiful shapes. These spiders use special body parts to make silk for their webs. The webs trap insects for them to eat. Many spiders add a sticky glue to the web. This makes it hard for insects to escape. Once an insect is caught, the spider wraps it tightly in silk.
pages.brief: A spider spins a beautiful web between plants, using silk from its body. Sticky drops of glue shine on the threads, and a trapped insect struggles. The spider wraps another caught insect tightly in silk.

pages.text: Spider silk is stronger than steel. You can easily break a web because the threads are so thin. If the threads were as thick as a rope, the web would be strong enough to lift a jet airplane!
pages.brief: A close-up photograph shows thin, delicate spider silk threads in a web. A separate comparison image shows a thick rope made of silk lifting a jet airplane, illustrating how strong spider silk would be if the threads were as thick as a rope.

pages.text: Some spiders also use their silk as a way to travel. Wind can blow the silk across a space, and it sticks to the other side. Spiders use the silk thread to walk from one twig or leaf to another.
pages.brief: A spider stands on a twig as a strand of silk is blown by the wind across an open space and sticks to a leaf on the other side. The spider then walks along the silk thread from one twig to another.

pages.text: Some baby spiders make a silk parachute to travel. The wind carries the piece of silk and lifts the spider with it. A parachute can carry a baby spider from just a short distance to over 100 kilometers (62 mi.).
pages.brief: A tiny baby spider releases a piece of silk into the wind, and the silk acts like a parachute, lifting the spider into the air. The spider drifts over a wide outdoor landscape, able to travel a short distance or more than 100 kilometers.

pages.text: Some Cool Spiders Many spiders do not spin webs to catch prey. The spitting spider, for example, spits sticky liquid onto its prey. This liquid becomes hard and traps the insect, like a net. The jumping spider can jump from far away to surprise and attack its prey.
pages.brief: A spitting spider shoots sticky liquid from its mouth onto an insect, and the liquid hardens into a net-like trap. Nearby, a jumping spider leaps from a distance toward its prey, surprising and attacking it.

pages.text: A trapdoor spider peeks up out of its hole in the ground. The spider springs out of its hole, surprising its prey. The trapdoor spider digs a hole in the ground and covers it with silk. This spider springs up out of the trapdoor when an insect walks by. Tarantulas also spring out of holes in the ground to catch insects. Some tarantulas catch even bigger meals, such as birds and lizards.
pages.brief: A trapdoor spider peeks out from a silk-covered hole in the ground, then springs up to surprise an insect walking past. Nearby, a tarantula also springs from a ground hole, ready to catch an insect or even a bird or lizard.

pages.text: Other Cool Spiders Name Body Length Home Unusual Traits Goldenrod crab spider 4–8 millimeters (0.16–0.3 in.) The goldenrod crab spider hides in flowers to attack bees. It can change color to match the flower it is in. North America, Europe, Northern Asia Red-rump tarantula 5.0–7.5 centimeters (2–3 in.) The red-rump tarantula defends itself by shooting out sharp hairs with hooks at the ends, which can cause an itchy rash. North America Water spider 8–15 millimeters (0.3–0.6 in.) The water spider fills an underwater web with air bubbles so it can breathe. Europe, Northern Asia Mirror spider The mirror spider may look like a disco ball! Shiny patches on its body scatter light to help it hide from enemies. 2.5–4 millimeters (0.1–0.16 in.) Southeast Asia, Australia Bird dropping crab spider 2.5–12 millimeters (0.1–0.5 in.) The bird dropping crab spider attracts insects by looking and smelling like a pile of bird poop. Southeast Asia Ladybug mimic spider 10 millimeters (0.4 in.) Asia The ladybug mimic spider keeps safe from enemies by looking just like a ladybug, which has a bad taste.
pages.brief: A photo grouping shows six spiders from different regions: a goldenrod crab spider hiding in a flower and changing color, a red-rump tarantula shooting sharp hairs, a water spider with air bubbles underwater, a shiny mirror spider, a bird-dropping look-alike crab spider, and a ladybug mimic spider.

pages.text: Spiders are unusual animals. They build beautiful webs, have powerful venom, and can sail through the air on silk. We depend on spiders to keep harmful insects under control. These skillful creatures have an important place in our natural world.
pages.brief: Several spiders are shown in a natural setting: one on a beautiful web, one with powerful venom, and baby spiders sailing through the air on silk. Around them are insects that spiders help keep under control, showing the important place these creatures have in the natural world.

books.title: A Prairie Dog's Life
books.art_why: Prairie dogs are real animals that can be photographed today.

pages.text: A Prairie Dog’s Life.
pages.brief: A black-tailed prairie dog stands upright on a short-grass prairie beside a low dirt mound, looking out over open land. The sky is wide and bright, and the animal’s fur and alert posture are clearly visible in a natural setting.

pages.text: The Big Day Spring has come to the prairie. Today, Charlie will go outside for the first time. Charlie has lived his first few months below ground. Charlie is a black-tailed prairie dog. But is he really a dog? No! Prairie dogs are actually squirrels, part of the rodent family.
pages.brief: Inside a warm underground burrow, a small black-tailed prairie dog named Charlie rests in the dim light. Above him is the spring prairie, and today will be his first time going outside after living below ground.

pages.text: Pioneers named the prairie dog because they thought the animal’s call sounded like a dog’s bark. Charlie loves his warm, cozy burrow, but he wants to go outside. Lucky Charlie! Today his mother will take him and his three sisters above ground. They will learn about the big world outside.
pages.brief: Charlie’s mother stands at the burrow entrance with Charlie and his three sisters close beside her. They are ready to climb above ground together, leaving the warm, cozy burrow to learn about the wide prairie world outside.

pages.text: Welcome to the Prairie The “prairie” part of Charlie’s name comes from his habitat. All of the world’s grasslands, or prairies, have burrowing mammals that create underground homes. In the United States, that animal is the prairie dog. When he is grown, Charlie will weigh 1.5 to 3 pounds (0.68-1.36 kg). Standing on his rear feet, he will be about 1 foot tall (30.48 cm). That is about the size of a large squirrel or a guinea pig.
pages.brief: Charlie stands on short prairie grass, shown small beside a large squirrel and a guinea pig to suggest his future size. Around him stretch open grasslands with burrowing mammals, and his burrow opening sits nearby in the flat, grassy habitat.

pages.text: There are five types of prairie dog. They are the Gunnison’s, black- tailed, white-tailed, Mexican, and Utah prairie dogs. The black-tailed are the most common, living on lowland prairies. Gunnison’s Black-tailed White-tailed Utah Mexican.
pages.brief: Five black-tailed, Gunnison’s, white-tailed, Mexican, and Utah prairie dogs stand on lowland prairie grass, each type grouped in its own area. The black-tailed prairie dogs are the most numerous, gathered on open lowland ground under a broad sky.

pages.text: MAP KEY ND MT Prairie dog species SD Black-tailed WY NE Gunnison’s UT CO KS Utah White-tailed OK NM AZ Mexican TX These areas are where the five types of prairie dogs make their homes. Mexico PACIFIC OCEAN Home Below Ground Charlie’s underground home is called a coterie (KOH-tur-ee). Each family has its own small coterie, a hole that is made up of small “rooms.” Many coteries together make a prairie dog colony. One colony can spread for hundreds of miles and house thousands of dogs!
pages.brief: A large map of the central United States shows shaded regions where five kinds of prairie dogs make their homes. Below it, a cutaway view reveals an underground coterie with small rooms, connected to a sprawling colony of many burrows.

pages.text: Charlie and his sisters poke their noses outside their burrow. The sun is so bright compared to the dark underground. But it is wonderful! They climb out of their burrow and over the mound of dirt at its opening. All around them is short prairie grass and plants. A Prairie Dog’s Life.
pages.brief: Charlie and his sisters climb out of their burrow and over the dirt mound at its opening. Bright sunlight makes them squint after the dark underground. All around them grow short prairie grass and low plants under a wide, open sky.

pages.text: Charlie’s Underground Home a) main mound b) listening post c) toilet d) “dry room” for floods Do You Know? One prairie dog colony in western Texas grew to be 100 miles wide and 250 miles long (161 km by 402 km). It was estimated that 400 million prairie dogs lived there.
pages.brief: A cutaway view shows Charlie’s underground home: a main mound above ground, a listening post, a toilet area, and a dry room for floods. Tunnels and small rooms connect within the earth beneath the prairie grass, forming a safe network below the surface.

pages.text: Danger! Charlie and his sisters begin to explore. Before long, a prairie dog’s sharp bark cuts through the air. “Yee-ipp!” he shouts with a hop. He has spotted danger! “Yee-ipp!” Charlie’s father replies. All of the prairie dogs stand tall, alert. Even though there is danger, they stay. The dogs will stay very still and watch until the danger goes away. A Prairie Dog’s Life.
pages.brief: A prairie dog stands tall with a hop and barks a sharp warning across the short grass. Charlie’s father answers with another bark. All around, prairie dogs stand alert and very still, watching for danger instead of running away.

pages.text: What might the danger be? Many predators hunt prairie dogs. Predators include coyotes, bobcats, prairie falcons, black-footed ferrets, and golden eagles.
pages.brief: Several predators appear on the prairie: a coyote, a bobcat, a prairie falcon, a black-footed ferret, and a golden eagle. They are shown as dangers that hunt prairie dogs, watching or swooping near the grassy burrow area.

pages.text: Perhaps the biggest danger of all is humans. Some people think prairie dogs destroy the land. These people try to harm prairie dogs by destroying their homes or killing them. Other people believe prairie dogs are important because their burrows bring air and water to the soil. Burrows also provide hiding places for other animals to escape predators. A Prairie Dog’s Life.
pages.brief: People stand on the prairie near prairie dog burrows. Some look disapprovingly at the burrows, while others point to the holes as helpful to the soil and as hiding places for other animals to escape predators.

pages.text: Summertime for Charlie Not all yips and barks signal danger. Some yips or barks signal a prairie dog is lonely or upset. Now Charlie hears more yips and barks from the older prairie dogs that signal it is safe. The threat is gone. Charlie and his sisters like playing outside in the sun. They will spend most of their summer outside.
pages.brief: Charlie and his sisters play outside in the warm summer sun. Nearby, older prairie dogs yip and bark softly, signaling that the threat is gone. The prairie is safe again, and the young prairie dogs spend most of the summer above ground.

pages.text: As summer turns to fall, they will prepare their burrow for winter. During winter, they will rarely go out into the harsh weather. Early next spring, the older females will have babies. And in late spring, Charlie will be an adult male. He will share in the watchdog duties. He will probably start a family and build his own coterie. A Prairie Dog’s Life.
pages.brief: As summer turns to fall, prairie dogs prepare their burrow for winter. In the cold months they stay mostly underground. The next spring, older females will have babies, and Charlie will grow into an adult male with watchdog duties and his own coterie.

books.title: Sound All Around
books.art_why: Sound, ears and instruments are real-world science topics that photographs can show accurately.

pages.text: What Makes Sound? Crash, boom, bam, bang, swoosh, and splash —sounds are all around us.
pages.brief: An outdoor scene alive with sound: a wave splashing hard against rocks, a heavy object crashing down, and a rush of wind sweeping past. Bursts of motion show the force of each crash, boom and splash, filling the air all around.

pages.text: People, animals, and objects make sounds. Even the weather makes sound. Sounds can be loud or soft. They can be pleasant or unpleasant.
pages.brief: A lively scene where sound comes from many sources: a person talking and clapping, a dog barking, a drum being struck, and rain falling with thunder overhead. Some sounds look loud and jolting, others soft and gentle, pleasant and unpleasant together.

pages.text: Animals use sound in many ways. Humans use sound to communicate their thoughts and feelings. Other animals use sound to communicate, too. They use sound to defend themselves, attract a mate, or signal a warning.
pages.brief: Several animals using sound: a songbird calling to attract a mate, a cat hissing with bared teeth to defend itself, and a group of animals standing alert at a warning cry. Each creature opens its mouth or listens, communicating through sound in its own way.

pages.text: Humans have invented many things to make sounds. Drums, bagpipes, and stringed instruments make music. Horns, bells, and sirens sound warnings or call people to events. Alarm clocks signal with music or loud beeps that it is time to get out of bed.
pages.brief: A collection of sound-making inventions: drums, bagpipes and stringed instruments played for music; horns, bells and a siren sounding a warning; and an alarm clock on a bedside table buzzing loudly to wake someone. Hands strike and blow, filling the scene with noise.

pages.text: What Is Sound? Sound is made when an object vibrates, or moves back and forth very quickly. People make sound to talk when air vibrates vocal cords in their throats. Different vibrations in the vocal cords make different sounds.
pages.brief: A close view of a person speaking, one hand at the throat where vocal cords vibrate. Ripples of air spread outward from the mouth. Beside this, an object quivers quickly back and forth, showing the fast vibration that makes sound.

pages.text: Try This! Feel the Vibration • Get two rubber bands, one thick and one thin. • Stretch them over an open shoebox. • Pluck each rubber band. • Listen to the sounds they make. • How are the sounds different? Why?
pages.brief: Hands stretch a thick rubber band and a thin rubber band over an open shoebox, then pluck each one. The bands blur with vibration as they snap back and forth, and a listening face leans close, comparing the two different sounds the plucked bands make.

pages.text: A vibrating object makes the air around it move. This is how sound travels. It moves outward in all directions. For example, when a tree crashes to the ground, the air around it vibrates. When the vibrating air reaches your ear, you hear the sound of a crashing tree. The vibrating air is called sound waves. Sound waves also travel through solids and liquids.
pages.brief: A tall tree crashes to the forest floor, and rings of vibrating air spread outward from it in every direction. The ripples travel through the air toward a person standing nearby, whose ear catches the sound of the falling tree.

pages.text: Different Sounds Not all sound is alike. Some sounds are loud. Others are quiet. The loudness of sound is called volume. The more air that vibrates, the louder the volume. For example, a lion’s roar vibrates more air than a buzzing bee’s wings. Sound also can be high or low. This is called pitch. Pitch depends on how fast something vibrates. Sirens vibrate quickly and have a high pitch. Bass drums vibrate slowly and have a low pitch.
pages.brief: A lion roars with its mouth wide, sending a big, loud sound, while a tiny bee buzzes nearby with soft wings. On the other side, a siren blares a high, quick sound and a bass drum is struck with a slow, low boom.

pages.text: Math Minute It takes sound about five seconds to travel one mile.
pages.brief: A wide outdoor view with a long stretch of ground and a clock face showing five seconds, as spreading sound waves cross the distance. The scene shows how far sound travels in a short time.

pages.text: Ears and Sound The outside of your ear is shaped to collect sound waves. The sound waves move from outside the ear to inside the ear. Tiny bones inside vibrate when they are struck by sound waves. The vibrating bones send messages through nerves to your brain. Your brain then interprets the messages as noise, music, talking, or other sounds.
pages.brief: A large view of an ear: the outer curve collects incoming sound waves, which travel inside to tiny bones that quiver. From the bones, thin nerves carry signals onward to a brain, where the messages become noise, music, talking and other sounds.

pages.text: The inner parts of the ear are very sensitive. Very loud sounds can hurt your ears. Be careful around loud noises. Cover your ears with your hands, or wear coverings on your ears such as earphones or earplugs. Or simply move away from the loud sounds.
pages.brief: A person presses both hands over their ears near a very loud noise, face tense. Nearby, someone wears earplugs and another walks away from the sound. The inner ear is shown as delicate and easily hurt by loud sounds.

pages.text: Conclusion We are surrounded by sounds. Vibrations make loud, quiet, high, and low sounds. Our ears pick up these sounds, and our brain tells us what they are. Enjoy the many sounds of the world and be careful with your ears!
pages.brief: A person stands outdoors surrounded by many sounds: birds calling, music playing, people talking and everyday noises rising and falling. Vibrations of high, low, loud and quiet sounds fill the air, and the person listens happily while keeping hands ready to guard their ears.

books.title: Louis Braille: A Man and His Method
books.art_why: It is a biography of a named famous person, Louis Braille.

pages.text: The Accident In 1809, Louis Braille was born in a small town in the country of France. One day at the age of three, Louis hurt himself. While playing in his father’s shoe workshop, he tried to make his own pair of shoes.
pages.brief: Young Louis Braille in a small town in France in 1809, playing in his father’s shoe workshop. At age three, he tries to make his own pair of shoes. He holds his father’s sharp awl while bending over, and the accident happens.

pages.text: Louis picked up his father’s sharp awl and bent over. The awl went into Louis’s eye. His hurt eye became sick. Before long, the sickness spread to his other eye. By age five, Louis could no longer see. He was blind.
pages.brief: Louis Braille bent over with his father’s sharp awl. The awl goes into his eye. His hurt eye becomes sick, and the sickness spreads to his other eye. By age five, Louis can no longer see and is blind.

pages.text: Louis went to school with children who could see. He learned by listening, but since he could not see, he could not read or write. Like many other parents of children who were blind back then, Louis’s parents feared for his future. However, when Louis was ten, they were able to send him to a special school in Paris.
pages.brief: Louis Braille goes to school with children who can see. He learns by listening, but cannot read or write. His parents fear for his future. When Louis is ten, they send him to a special school in Paris.

pages.text: A New Sort of School The school in Paris was for boys who were blind. It was one of the first such schools in the world. Louis learned many skills at this school. He learned how to weave branches together to make chairs. He learned how to sew leather to make slippers.
pages.brief: At the Paris school for boys who are blind, one of the first such schools in the world, Louis Braille learns many skills. He weaves branches together to make chairs and sews leather to make slippers.

pages.text: Louis also learned how to read. He felt raised letters on a sheet of paper. The paper was pressed against copper wires shaped like letters. This made raised letters on the paper that fingers could feel. But the letters were difficult to read. Too many letters had similar shapes and felt the same. And the wire used to make these letters had to be shaped by people who could see. It seemed there had to be a better way for people who were blind to read.
