pages.brief: Louis Braille learns to read by feeling raised letters on paper. The paper was pressed against copper wires shaped like letters. The letters are hard to read because many feel the same. People who can see must shape the wires, so a better way seems needed.

pages.text: Night Writing Charles Barbier, a soldier, invented a form of night writing for France’s army. Soldiers often hid in the dark. They did not want to use a light because they did not want to be found. Night writing used twelve small raised dots to form each letter. It gave soldiers a way to read in the dark. It also allowed soldiers to send messages to one another without using light or making a noise. This code was too hard for most soldiers to learn, however. The army decided not to use it, so in 1821, Barbier took the system to Louis’s school.
pages.brief: Charles Barbier, a soldier, invents night writing for France’s army. Soldiers hide in the dark and avoid light so they are not found. Night writing uses twelve small raised dots for each letter, letting soldiers read and send messages silently. The army decides not to use it, and in 1821 Barbier brings it to Louis’s school.

pages.text: Louis believed a system of raised dots could be used to help people who are blind to read. He had been trying to create a touch system of his own for reading and writing. When he tried night writing, he knew it was the right idea but was also too difficult.
pages.brief: Louis Braille believes raised dots can help people who are blind read. He has been trying to create his own touch system for reading and writing. When he tries night writing, he knows it is the right idea but also too difficult.

pages.text: The night-writing system did not allow a fingertip to touch a whole letter. Readers had to move their finger to feel the whole symbol. Night writing also did not include periods, question marks, music signs, or numbers. Louis asked Barbier to change his system to make it easier, but the soldier would not change it.
pages.brief: Night writing does not let a fingertip touch a whole letter; readers must move a finger to feel the whole symbol. It lacks periods, question marks, music signs, and numbers. Louis Braille asks Barbier to change his system and make it easier, but the soldier will not change it.

pages.text: Louis’s Own System Over a few years, Louis made a shorter, easier form of this touch system. He used six dots instead of twelve to form each letter. It allowed a person’s fingertip to feel the entire symbol without having to move. This difference let people who are blind read much more quickly and easily.
pages.brief: Over a few years, Louis Braille makes a shorter, easier touch system. He uses six dots instead of twelve to form each letter. A person’s fingertip can feel the entire symbol without moving. This difference lets people who are blind read much more quickly and easily.

pages.text: At age fifteen, Louis shared this new system with his classmates and the school. Several years later, Louis added similar dot codes for music and math. Today, we call this form of written language braille. It is named after Louis Braille, who helped invent it. Now, people who are blind use a stylus and a slate to write braille. Dots are punched on the back of heavy paper with a stylus. A slate is used to keep the dots spaced correctly. Sentences are written from right to left. Then the paper is flipped over, and the sentences are read from left to right.
pages.brief: At age fifteen, Louis Braille shares his new system with classmates and the school. Later he adds dot codes for music and math. Today this written language is called braille, named after him. People who are blind use a stylus and slate, punching dots on heavy paper from right to left, then flipping the paper to read left to right.

pages.text: Braille can also be written using a Perkins Brailler, a typewriter-like machine. Braille gives people who are blind a way to both read and write. From Stylus to Smartphone The invention of smartphones has led to many apps that help people who can’t see. As a result, far fewer people who are blind can read braille today than in the past two centuries—only one in ten. The same rule applies to braille as any other language: use it or lose it.
pages.brief: Braille can be written with a Perkins Brailler, a typewriter-like machine. Braille gives people who are blind a way to read and write. Smartphones have led to apps that help people who cannot see. Far fewer people who are blind read braille today, only one in ten; the rule is use it or lose it.

pages.text: A Loved Teacher Braille became a teacher at the school he attended as a child. He was loved by his students. He died in 1852, but his form of writing lives on. Even though Louis Braille became blind at a young age, he never gave up. Instead, he overcame great obstacles, which made it possible for people who are blind to read.
pages.brief: Louis Braille becomes a teacher at the school he attended as a child. He is loved by his students. He dies in 1852, but his form of writing lives on. Though he became blind young, Louis never gave up and overcame great obstacles, making it possible for people who are blind to read.
